- [同一周里，四个开源项目对 AI 贡献给出了四种答案：分歧不在技术，而在「声明」到底有什么用](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-10-15_open-source-ai-contribution-policies-compared/): Analysis of four open-source projects that reached different conclusions about AI-assisted contributions between July and October 2026, plus LLVM's competing proposal. Details GCC's policy announced 29 July 2026 declining any legally significant contribution containing or derived from LLM-generated content, where legally significant follows the GNU maintainer guidelines threshold of roughly 15 lines of code or text, with exceptions for legally insignificant changes (requiring normal contribution standards and clear disclosure) and for legally significant LLM-generated test cases handled separately because they are small programs reproducing compiler bugs; notes GCC permits LLM use for discussing ideas, understanding existing code, research and analysis and bug discovery as long as generated material is not included in contributions, records that human cleanup does not change the policy's reach, traces the working group from creation on 16 April 2026 through SC approval on 24 April with Jonathan Wakely leading and meetings ending 3 July to the 29 July announcement, and preserves the dissent from Richard Biener that the policy grounds rejection in legal issues while leaving the far more severe issues of overwhelming reviewers and keeping GCC maintainable unaddressed, with Arthur Cohen's reply that such contributions are disallowed so no reviewer time is burned. Covers the Linux kernel's reversal: the Assisted-by tag requirement introduced around December 2025 with a format naming agent and model version, deprecated by consensus at the Maintainers Summit in Prague on 8 October 2026 and removed by Sasha Levin's patch on 9 October (4 files, one insertion, 51 deletions), with the three reasons Jeff Layton gave earlier in July (not universally followed, effectively free advertising for proprietary LLM companies, and unclear why the information was being collected at all) and Christian Brauner's sharper version that git history had started to function like an advertising platform for AI companies and their proprietary agents and models; the kernel's rule that AI agents MUST NOT add Signed-off-by tags because only humans can legally certify the DCO stays unchanged. Covers Debian's General Resolution with discussion from 23 July, voting from 15 to 28 August 2026 and results on 30 August, where the winning option states Debian neither endorses nor prohibits generative AI tools, expects all contributions to meet the same standards of quality correctness maintainability and legal compliance, holds that using a generative AI tool does not diminish the contributor's responsibility, encourages but does not require disclosure, and explicitly declines to resolve the unsettled legal status of AI-generated material; notes the proposal's acknowledgement of inspiration from GCC's AI policy and rust-lang's LLM usage policy. Covers Flathub's reversal from a May 2026 blanket ban after a 4 September policy revision, with the new text requiring disclosure identifying affected parts and approximate extent, prohibiting AI content in manifests with disclosure not exempting them, exempting research discussion and debugging uses where no generated material is included, leaving disclosed material to reviewer discretion, stating that disclosure does not create a presumption of acceptance, banning AI tools or agents from opening or automating submission pull requests or generating commit messages descriptions review comments or replies, and allowing permanent bans for repeated violations. Adds LLVM's 5 October RFC to ban AI-generated or substantially AI-assisted textual communication including PR descriptions while leaving code rules unchanged, motivated by the point that AI-written descriptions deprive contributors of understanding what a PR does and expressing it themselves as a sanity check on the human-in-the-loop model, and records its lesson that the earlier policy which strongly encouraged writing PR descriptions oneself turned out to be essentially useless. Argues the four policies do not disagree about whether AI is allowed but about whether disclosure is useful and who bears the verification cost: GCC filters with a measurable 15-line threshold so disclosure is redundant, the kernel found disclosure had no purpose and side effects, Debian keeps the information optional and relies on responsibility, and Flathub needs disclosure as an input because reviewers use it to decide how deeply to examine a submission; generalises this to asking what you will do differently once you receive a disclosure. Identifies the one thing all four agree on, that responsibility must rest on a specific human, with the kernel's phrasing being the most precise because DCO is a legal declaration that only a subject with legal capacity can make, and notes this shifts the governance problem to human review capacity, which GCC's minority view and Asterinas's aster-code-review skill are the two places actually addressing.
  - Key topics: GCC AI policy, legally significant, 15 lines, LLM-generated content, derived from, GNU maintainer guidelines, AI policy working group, Jonathan Wakely, Richard Biener, Arthur Cohen, Linux kernel Assisted-by, Sasha Levin, Maintainers Summit Prague, Jeff Layton, Christian Brauner, free advertising, Signed-off-by, DCO, Debian General Resolution, Social Contract, neither endorses nor prohibits, disclosure encouraged not required, Flathub generative AI policy, disclosure does not create a presumption of acceptance, reviewer discretion, LLVM RFC AI-generated communication, human in the loop, human review bandwidth, 译文

- [CISA 要停掉每周漏洞通报：一句「BOD 26-04」说得通吗？](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-09-19_cisa-ends-vuln-bulletin/): Translation+analysis of CSO Online's report (Maxwell Cooter, 2026-09-18). CISA will stop its weekly known-vulnerability bulletin from 2026-09-28, officially attributing the move to Binding Operational Directive BOD 26-04, which requires federal agencies to prioritize patching by real-world risk factors (evidence of in-the-wild exploitation) rather than severity scores. The article questions why complying with BOD precludes continuing the weekly bulletin — the two are not mutually exclusive, so the real driver is likely resource contraction or the surge in AI-generated threats (CISA warned earlier this month about attackers targeting AI assets). CISA will still publish via KEV, Cybersecurity Alerts and Advisories, and the CVE catalog, and urges CISOs to watch vendors' own security bulletins. Takeaways: the real change is the prioritization pivot from CVSS to in-the-wild exploitation (consistent with KEV); the BOD justification is weak; frontline teams should subscribe KEV into their monitoring and track vendor advisories instead of relying on a weekly email.
  - Key topics: CISA, vulnerability management, BOD 26-04, KEV, vulnerability prioritization, CVSS, security operations, US government

### 安全/漏洞

- [不到两周，X.Org 又发了 17 个 CVE：而这一次全在客户端库里，威胁模型反过来了](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-10-16_xorg-17-cves-client-libraries/): Translation+analysis of X.Org's security advisory published 16 October 2026 by Alan Coopersmith and Phoronix's coverage, covering seventeen CVEs across five X client libraries: libX11 fixed in 1.8.14 with four, libXi fixed in 1.8.4 with nine, libXpm fixed in 3.5.20, libXrender fixed in 0.9.13 with one, and libXtst fixed in 1.2.6, against a backdrop where a dozen X.Org Server and XWayland vulnerabilities were published less than two weeks earlier. Lays out the individual CVEs that can be verified: CVE-2026-88806 as an out-of-bounds write in libX11's XKB action parser where a malicious server can send an XkbGetMap reply with keycode values exceeding max_keycode plus one causing writes past the allocated array, rated 7.5 and found by Adam Bedard with TrendAI's Zero Day Initiative; CVE-2026-94283 and CVE-2026-94284 as out-of-bounds reads in the XIM attribute parser and trigger-key registration parser where a malicious or compromised XIM server sends inconsistent nested attribute lengths, found by Aisle Research and rated 6.5 and 5.5; CVE-2026-94285 as an out-of-bounds read in the byte-oriented codeset parser; the libXi group including CVE-2026-93541 where XQueryDeviceState trusts the num_valuators value from a ValuatorClass reply without checking it fits the declared class, CVE-2026-93545 and CVE-2026-94281 in XListInputDevices, CVE-2026-94282 in XI2 enter/leave/focus cookie conversion, and XI2 XIQueryDevice reply parsing; CVE-2026-88807 as the most severe of the batch, a heap overflow in libXrender's RenderQueryPictFormats where a numSubpixels count greater than the number of screens causes an out-of-bounds write, described by NVD and OpenCVE as usable by a malicious X server to inject code into attached X clients and rated 8.3; CVE-2026-94286 as an out-of-bounds read in libXtst's RECORD reply parser rated 7.1; and CVE-2026-94287 as an unsigned underflow in libXpm's write path enabling denial of service, already fixed in Ubuntu via USN-8862-1. Then makes the central argument that the batch's significance is not its size but its direction: X11's historical hardening has been about protecting the server from malicious clients, since a client can read the whole screen, inject keystrokes and capture windows, so protections like XSECURITY, XACE and eventually Wayland's design all point that way, whereas seven of these advisories describe a malicious server attacking a client, which raises the question of why that direction is now real and answers it with three concrete settings (ssh -X remote forwarding where the far end is a server you do not fully control, nested X servers such as Xephyr and Xwayland setups where an intermediate layer may be untrusted, and containers or untrusted display services), then explains why most of the batch are out-of-bounds reads rather than writes since a length-versus-content mismatch is enough to read past a buffer while writing past one requires controlling a value used as an index or length, which also explains the cluster of CVSS scores in the 5 to 7 range whose consequence is crashing a client rather than taking it over, with CVE-2026-88807 as the exception precisely because it is a write. Quotes three technical descriptions that expose the shared pattern of trusting a value from a reply without validating it, including the num_valuators check, the max_keycode plus one bound, and numSubpixels exceeding screen count, noting that the recurring primitives are num_valuators, numSubpixels, nested XIM attribute lengths and XKB keycode. Places the batch in 2026's cadence with the April, July and early-October rounds listed, and asks whether the density reflects stricter auditing or older code, answering both since commercial vulnerability research and independent scanning are both active while the affected code paths in XIM, XKB and XRender date from the 1990s. Gives operators a risk table keyed on whether the malicious-server premise holds in their environment, treating plain local desktop use as routine patching while prioritising ssh -X, nested X and untrusted display services, and noting that containers where you are defending against clients are a different direction entirely. Adds the observation that the oldest of these vulnerabilities all live in extensions rather than the core protocol, which was designed more cautiously and audited earlier, and closes by noting Wayland's transition has not removed the X11 attack surface but relocated it into the compatibility layer, since XWayland depends on these same client libraries and the early-October batch affected both server and XWayland.
  - Key topics: X.Org, X client libraries, libX11, libXi, libXpm, libXrender, libXtst, X.Org Server, XWayland, CVE-2026-88806, CVE-2026-94283, CVE-2026-94284, CVE-2026-94285, CVE-2026-93541, CVE-2026-93545, CVE-2026-94281, CVE-2026-94282, CVE-2026-88807, CVE-2026-94286, CVE-2026-94287, CVE-2026-4367, CVE-2026-55999, CVE-2026-56000, XKB, XkbGetMap, max_keycode, XIM, XIM_OPEN_REPLY, XIM_REGISTER_TRIGGERKEYS, XRenderQueryFormat, RenderQueryPictFormats, numSubpixels, num_valuators, XQueryDeviceState, XListInputDevices, XIQueryDevice, RECORD, XTEST, out-of-bounds read, out-of-bounds write, heap overflow, denial of service, threat model, malicious server, malicious client, XSECURITY, XACE, ssh -X, Xephyr, Xwayland, ZDI, TrendAI, Adam Bedard, Aisle Research, Alan Coopersmith, Oracle, Peter Hutterer, USN-8862-1, CVSS, Wayland


- [三十五年后重读《Why I Wrote PGP》：它讲的不是加密，而是「一次变更由谁发起」](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-10-16_why-i-wrote-pgp-revisited/): Translation+analysis of Philip Zimmermann's 1991 essay updated in 1999, reading it in its own argument order and noting an access quirk that the site worked over a direct connection while failing through the HTTP proxy. Leads with why the essay still persuades: it locates the problem in a changed cost structure rather than a moral claim, with the fishing-line versus driftnet contrast showing that labour-intensive monitoring was impractical at scale as a physical fact which then dissolved once computing power grew, while law and ethics did not update alongside it. Covers the envelope-and-postcard argument, including the argument that a mailing everything on postcards world would make using an envelope itself suspicious, so there is safety in numbers and routine universal encryption removes the signal; notes this holds even more strongly today for metadata, where the existence, frequency, timing and counterparties of communication remain visible even when content is encrypted, making privacy a phenomenon requiring scale rather than an individual choice. Establishes the trigger from the public record: Senate Bill 266 in the 102nd Congress, the Comprehensive Counter-Terrorism Act of 1991 introduced by Senator Biden on 24 January 1991, whose Subtitle B expressed the sense of Congress that providers and manufacturers should ensure systems permit the government to obtain plain text contents when appropriately authorised, noting it was a non-binding sense-of-Congress provision that never became law and that EFF reported the encryption clause was removed from the replacement crime bill in June 1991, alongside Zimmermann's own account of racing to publish before publishing such software became illegal. Records the three subsequent events: the Clipper chip announced in April 1993 with a classified NSA algorithm and keys held in escrow subject to a promise of use only when duly authorised, the strong public and industry reaction, and Louis Freeh's shift from voluntary adoption to seeking legislative relief, including his testimony after the Oklahoma City bombing that public availability of strong cryptography must be curtailed even though nobody suggested the bombers used cryptography; and CALEA in 1994 mandating remote wiretap ports in central office switches, with the FBI's subsequent plan to build in capacity to wiretap one percent of all calls in major cities, which was defeated in Congress. Singles out as the most durable judgement the line that technology infrastructures can persist for generations while laws and policies can change overnight, and applies it as a checklist item to four present cases with the same shape (CALEA's remote wiretap ports, Intel ME and AMD PSP in the x86 boot path, cross-app persistent advertising identifiers, and the mutable-name trust binding in npm's Trusted Publishing), where each design decision was reasonable at the time and each capability outlived the legal environment it was made under. Covers the deployment-as-argument strategy of using strong cryptography as much as possible while it was still legal, its stated rationale that widespread use makes criminalisation harder, its recorded outcome in the 1999 export policy reversal, and the two conditions it depends on, namely that mass adoption is reversible and that popularisation itself is the desired result, which distinguishes PGP from cases like advertising identifiers where diffusion is the problem; and preserves the cost to the author, who faced a three-year criminal investigation after PGP spread worldwide before the case was dropped in early 1996. Closes by connecting the essay to the current round of AI contribution policies, arguing both answer how a system's defaults should change when a new capability becomes cheap, and that deployment-as-argument and explicit boundary-setting are appropriate in different situations, with the test being whether a world where everyone uses it is better or worse.
  - Key topics: PGP, Philip Zimmermann, Why I Wrote PGP, privacy, cryptography, cypherpunks, crypto wars, Senate Bill 266, Comprehensive Counter-Terrorism Act 1991, sense of Congress, plain text contents, trapdoor, key escrow, Clipper chip, NSA, Skipjack, Louis Freeh, FBI, COINTELPRO, CALEA, wiretap ports, Oklahoma City, EFF, EFFector Online, Patrick Leahy, export controls, deployment as argument, safety in numbers, envelope and postcard, driftnet fishing, metadata, Intel ME, AMD PSP, advertising identifier, npm Trusted Publishing, AgFection, 译文


- [RPKI 覆盖涨到 70%，而它没能拦住的恰恰是一次真实劫持：因为那次攻击是「RPKI 有效」的](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-10-16_rpki-70-percent-coverage-hetzner-hijack/): Translation+analysis of IPinfo's routing measurement report and several primary sources it corroborates. Reports the headline that the share of routed prefixes that are RPKI-valid rose from 54.0 percent in September 2025 to 70.3 percent a year later, a gain of 16.4 points against three to four points in each of the two prior years, and that invalid routes barely propagate, with a typical valid prefix seen by 596 vantage points, one with no RPKI record by 595, and an invalid one by just two. Shows the increase is highly concentrated: China went from 3.7 percent to 83.0 percent of its IPv4 addresses in valid routes, almost 60 percent of the global gain measured by addresses, most of it after the end of December 2025 when only 2.9 percent of its routed prefixes were valid, moving China from pulling the global average down in 2025 (53.1 worldwide against 58.0 excluding China) to pushing it up in 2026 (65.0 against 63.2); other large movers include Egypt from 23 to 99 percent, Kazakhstan from 16 to 84, Mexico from 37 to 78 and South Africa from 38 to 60. Notes IPv6 has overtaken IPv4 (valid prefixes rising from 56 to 79 percent against 54 to 68), contradicting a 2024 assessment by Job Snijders that IPv6 ROA growth seemed to be stalling, and that two metrics he flagged also reversed (address blocks per ROA from 2.31 to 2.62, and publication points from 73 to 91 as more organisations host their own repositories). Then pivots to the central tension: the August 2026 hijack of Hetzner space used to deliver a malicious Virtualizor update was RPKI-valid, because the ROA for 162.55.0.0/16 authorised origin AS24940 with maxLength 24 and the forged /24 announced exactly that origin at exactly that length, so full ROV deployment would not have blocked it; preserves the key line that nothing about RPKI failed because the ROA permitted it, and reconstructs the full chain from the more-specific announcement winning longest-prefix match, through passing Let's Encrypt domain validation for a certificate covering 26 Softaculous domains, to a backdoored update whose indicator of compromise is a systemd unit named java-jre-update.service, with one provider reporting five of 34 hypervisors compromised at root, and the honest note that the small number affected was due to roughly 10,600 withdrawals and flap dampening making diversion intermittent rather than to defences working, plus the independent flaw that Virtualizor's update client did not cryptographically verify packages. Covers the measurement of how common that posture is: of 855,217 RPKI-covered IPv4 routes, 138,698 or 16.2 percent have a ROA looser than the route announced with no more-specific route of their own filling the gap, 20.9 percent for IPv6, leaving roughly 18 million more-specific prefixes an attacker could announce today and come out RPKI-valid and uncontested, against RFC 9319's long-standing recommendation to leave maxLength unset; includes the striking provider comparison (Contabo 540 of 553 routes open, DigitalOcean 780 of 863, OVH 11.5 percent, Cablevision 98.1 percent, Shaw 96.5 percent, Bharti Airtel 85.0 percent) and the note that Hetzner tightened three prefixes after the incident while 49 of its 63 covered routes remain open. Covers the disappearance cases where coverage can vanish without an outage and nobody notices unless they look: Mauritius falling from 94.0 to 69.0 percent after SEACOM lost four of six ROAs including one covering roughly a million addresses, Saudi Telecom losing protection on 19 routes including six blocks totalling about 1.6 million addresses before recovery, and Orange Maroc's ROAs going missing twice and taking Morocco from 20 percent coverage to almost none and back. Documents a critical measurement trap where methods that inspect records one by one report hard failures for records that are still providing protection because a link to the parent certificate goes stale when a repository moves, while the validation that actually produces the router list walks down from the trust anchors, so counting failing records is not a measure of lost protection; notes IPinfo's own stated methodology that validity is the share of routed prefixes classified valid against the validated authorisation set rather than the validation status of individual objects. Covers ASPA arriving for path validation, with publishing networks rising 25-fold from 131 to 3,272 and growth arriving in steps that each follow a registry making signing available, and explains why the headline 6.2 to 9.7 percent needs decomposing since about six points is a structural floor from short paths always passing, leaving real progress at roughly 3.5 percent up from 0.1 percent, with most of the remainder unknown rather than failing; notes the attribution trap where mid-path gaps make one provider's stale record taint all its customers' routes so ranking by origin blames the wrong party, that attributing by hop instead puts Cogent, Arelion and GTT at the top because declaring AS0 prevents a stale record further down from hiding as no attestation, and that Syrian Telecom's incomplete record alone accounts for 21 percent of all mid-path ASPA failures so the global failure rate is not yet a measure of Internet health. Also notes that nearly 60 percent of all routed IPv4 space not in RPKI-valid routes is in the United States with about a quarter belonging to the Department of Defense, and closes with the operational recommendations and the observation that this is what an infrastructure looks like once it matures, where the main problem shifts from whether to adopt to whether it is configured correctly.
  - Key topics: RPKI, ROA, ROV, BGP, route origin authorization, maxLength, RFC 9319, forged-origin hijack, longest prefix match, prefix hijack, Hetzner, AS24940, AS62390, NexonHost, AS6204, ZET.NET, Virtualizor, Softaculous, Let's Encrypt, TLS certificate, java-jre-update.service, hypervisor root compromise, IPinfo, RIPE RIS, RouteViews, vantage points, IPv4, IPv6, China, Egypt, Kazakhstan, Mexico, South Africa, publication points, Job Snijders, Contabo, DigitalOcean, OVH, Cablevision, Shaw, Bharti Airtel, SEACOM, Saudi Telecom, Orange Maroc, Mauritius, Morocco, measurement trap, trust anchor, stale certificate link, ASPA, AS0, Cogent, Arelion, GTT, Syrian Telecom, AS29386, AS201550, route leak, path validation, mis-origination, Department of Defense, 译文


- [同一份 AdFection 报告，这篇多给了企业一份可执行清单：而清单里最有效的一条，是「别把你的广告 ID 交出去」](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-10-16_adfection-enterprise-defense-checklist/): Analysis of Computerworld's CSO Online piece on the same Citizen Lab Report 195 already covered on this site, explicitly framed as the incremental value rather than a repeat of the technical mechanism. Leads with the report's own key operational conclusion, that you can directly block Discover-Tech's current methods by blocking advertising identifiers while the researchers suspect the AdFection attack surface may be larger and require more systematic measures, and explains why that works given that the NOAS server decides eligibility from a combination of source IP and advertising identifier. Adds the more precise figures the report contains, that ads with attacker script tags were shown to users of 75,373 different Android and iOS apps and to visitors of 120,768 different websites in mobile and desktop browsers, with the important qualifier that these refer to ads actually displayed rather than raw bids, differentiating them from the 3.77 billion bids and zero sales covered previously; names the highest-volume apps including MX Player and Lark Player above one million, Viber above 700,000, and Snap VPN, Truecaller and VivaCut each around half a million, plus deployment in Yahoo Mail and Opera Mini. Preserves three judgments from analyst Frank Dickson: that the ad carried no exploit at all and was clean which is the frightening part since nobody clicked anything, that in almost every case the server sent back nothing and only chosen targets received malicious code, and that third-party verification scanners saw a harmless banner because for nearly every viewer it was one, which is exactly how the tags slipped past verification; also his line that a certification is only as good as the vetting behind it. Highlights the sharpest observation of the piece, that many enterprises spend fortunes managing their users' identities and then let corporate phones hand that persistent identifier to anonymous auctions running hundreds of billions of times a day, with his conclusion that every ad is someone else's code running on your device and the ad network should be treated like any other untrusted vendor. Reproduces the enterprise checklist and adds why each item works: pushing a vetted ad-blocking extension through policy rather than leaving it to users, favouring browsers with built-in tracking protection, blocking ad and tracking domains at the DNS or secure web gateway layer because that reaches in-app ads on managed phones where browser extensions cannot, disabling advertising identifiers on corporate mobile devices through MDM and restricting ad-supported consumer apps on devices holding sensitive data, enabling Apple's Lockdown Mode for high-risk executives journalists and users travelling to sensitive locations, keeping browsers and operating systems patched because the ad is only the delivery truck and the exploit still needs a flaw, watching traffic tied to ad impressions for odd follow-on requests, and searching DNS and proxy logs for the domains published in the report. Includes the caveat that ad blockers are necessary but not wholly sufficient since many bids were for ads inside mobile apps that browser extensions typically overlook, and organises the checklist into control layers (browser extension, DNS or secure web gateway, MDM, Lockdown Mode, patch management) to show that each covers only part of the path so layering is what works. Distinguishes report findings from analyst inferences, noting that the identifier blocking claim is the report authors' judgment while disabling identifiers via MDM is Dickson's operational mapping whose applicability depends on whether the reader's MDM can actually control that setting and what turning it off breaks, and closes by arguing the value of the checklist is the vetting order it provides, first asking which layer reaches in-app ads, then which identifiers can be turned off, and only then working through logs.
  - Key topics: AdFection, Citizen Lab report 195, Discover-Tech, Controlium, Candiru, advertising identifier, mobile ad ID, cookie ID, IP address, NOAS server, 75,373 apps, 120,768 websites, MX Player, Lark Player, Viber, Snap VPN, Truecaller, VivaCut, Yahoo Mail, Opera Mini, Frank Dickson, Dickson Research, IDC, third-party verification scanner, self-attestation, certification vetting, MDM, ad blocking extension, tracking protection, DNS blocking, secure web gateway, in-app ads, Lockdown Mode, patch management, delivery truck, untrusted vendor, identity management paradox, DNS and proxy logs, 译文


- [微软把 Defender 装到了 Linux 桌面上：它卖的不是杀毒，而是「别让开发机成为你的可见性盲区」](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-10-16_microsoft-defender-linux-desktop-preview/): Translation+analysis of Microsoft's announcement and Phoronix's coverage of Microsoft Defender for Endpoint extending support from Linux servers to Linux desktops, correcting that the official documentation marks it Public Preview rather than general availability even though some coverage described it as released. Leads with Microsoft's stated reason being more informative than the product: that as more developers begin to use Linux desktops they become more attractive to attackers because they are high-privilege, high-value and easy for admins to overlook, with the argument that these three words form a complete chain since developer machines hold repository credentials, cloud API keys, SSH private keys and deployment rights, act as both a route into production and the location of source code, and become a problem precisely because they sit outside the administrator's view; concludes the product's substance is bringing devices that exist but are not on the list onto the list, and that this class of problem is never solved by stronger detection but by making the devices visible first. Covers the capability breakdown across protect and detect (endpoint detection and response, next-generation antivirus, threat analytics) and exposure management (asset inventory and Defender Vulnerability Management aiming at a consistent simplified view across the endpoint estate), and Microsoft's listed benefits including onboarding with deployment methods already validated for Linux servers, lower operational complexity from one agent and one security operations experience covering both desktops and servers, improved visibility across heterogeneous environments, stronger developer workstation security, and accelerated investigation and response. Explains why the absence of a desktop-specific agent matters: a separate agent would multiply every fix, detection and kernel compatibility effort across two agents in an ecosystem whose main complexity source is already the combination of distributions and kernel versions, so one agent means server-side compatibility work is reused directly. Explains why the desktop environment is deliberately not a variable in the support model, since EDR and antivirus care about processes, files, network connections and kernel interfaces which are identical across GNOME and KDE on the same distribution, while desktop environments only change who draws windows and manages sessions; notes this also clarifies that supporting Linux desktops means working correctly in desktop scenarios rather than understanding the desktop. Covers the licensing floor requiring standalone Defender for Endpoint Plan 2 or Microsoft 365 E5 and E7, which excludes individual users and small teams. Argues the supported distribution list (RHEL, CentOS, Ubuntu, Debian, SLES, Fedora, Oracle Linux with GNOME, KDE or other desktop environments) plus the licensing requirement sketch a specific enterprise customer profile, notes the functional set matches the server edition so it offers the same lens on more machines rather than new detection for developer scenarios, and connects this to the earlier point that agent-driven dependency installation changes the attack surface of developer machines in ways whose manifestation is a normal-looking package rather than a malicious process. States the unverified points honestly (no agent performance figures under desktop load, no specific kernel version range, and preview status meaning features and support scope can change), concludes the practical impact for individual users and small teams is close to zero while the real significance is confirming developer Linux workstations as objects that belong inside enterprise security management, and that this confirmation matters more than whether Microsoft supplies the tool.
  - Key topics: Microsoft, Defender, Defender for Endpoint, Linux desktop, Public Preview, EDR, next-generation antivirus, threat analytics, exposure management, Defender Vulnerability Management, asset inventory, high-privilege high-value easy to overlook, visibility gap, shared agent, GNOME, KDE, RHEL, CentOS, Ubuntu, Debian, SLES, Fedora, Oracle Linux, Defender for Endpoint Plan 2, Microsoft 365 E5, E7, licensing, developer workstation, Hyper-V, WSL, 译文


- [广告不是图片，是可执行代码：AdFection 用「先验身份、再发载荷」把实时竞价变成了一条零点击投毒通道](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-10-15_adfection-zero-click-spyware-targeted-ads/): Translation+analysis tracing a Financial Times story back to its primary source, the Citizen Lab's Report 195 published 15 October 2026 and a co-timed Confiant investigation, which together provide the first public technical confirmation of zero-click mercenary spyware delivered through targeted advertising, a technique they name AdFection (Ad plus Infection). Explains the core mechanism as two properties of the advertising ecosystem combined: RTB auctions collect granular device and user data and are designed to enable individual-level targeting by mobile advertising ID cookie ID or IP address, while ads are not merely images but containers that can run HTML and JavaScript from the advertiser DSP and other parties. Describes Discover-Tech's implementation where a winning bid pushes an ad containing a script tag pointing back to a NOAS or getAd server, the ad on render connects back and submits the user's advertising identifier, the server decides based on source IP and identifiers whether the target is eligible, returns JavaScript if so and a 0-byte response otherwise, and the returned code can load further code down to a browser exploit installing spyware; notes the report's statement that the mere display of a targeted ad is sufficient for infection and that the NOAS design lets Discover-Tech avoid sharing malicious code or even pointers to it with the companies that serve and display ads. Covers the confirmed case of at least 45 devices at Al Jazeera infected in 2024 and 2025 with Candiru spyware via Discover-Tech ads, with the temporal signature of contact with Discover-Tech domains for the ad impression, then a Candiru validator server for an initial check, then a Candiru command-and-control server, and explains that this staged design means nothing happens for non-targets and that the validator step mirrors long-standing phishing kit and watering hole practice now applied to a universal channel. Details the attribution evidence: the Fingerprint V1 validator banner matching 305 domains on 319 IP addresses between August 2022 and July 2026 including domains already attributed to Candiru by Sekoia and Recorded Future, the Fingerprint C1 command-and-control servers, and the isolated Windows DLL with SHA256 255869de85e2a171993fc5eb8a556d873a1b8966e040f6f55926f2fa2d595cc8 hardcoding two matching servers, concluding high confidence it is a newer version of the Candiru chain captured in 2021 on the basis of COM hijack persistence, a distinctive 48-byte repeating XOR obfuscation with a dummy null terminator that is silently discarded, and the same hardcoded connectivity check domains. Covers Controlium, the target-selection platform whose frontend source code was published on its own login page and which lets partners select a target by mobile advertising ID, browser cookie ID or IP address, along with the attribution clues (domains, the AWS load balancer CNAME, code strings, the ONLY DEKEL IS ALLOWED message at jsConfig, an unauthenticated endpoint exposing login data matching employees' names, and the caution that Discover-Tech branded some controlled ads with apparently unwitting third parties including Amazon and AliExpress for which there is no evidence they purchased the ads). Analyses the scale from nearly four billion bidding records: impressions across close to 200,000 apps and websites in dozens of countries, 3.77 billion bids over four months with zero recorded sales and about 109,091 dollars spent with all revenue and conversion fields zero, roughly ten million impressions daily per Confiant, only three advertisers in the database nearly all traceable to Discover-Tech or linked properties, and leading volumes by raw bids from Yemen and Pakistan and per capita from Montenegro; argues zero sales plus zero revenue plus heavy spend is itself a detectable commercial impossibility and that roughly 110,000 dollars bought targeting reach across 200,000 properties, explaining why the model is economically viable as cheap reconnaissance plus expensive weapons reserved for real targets. Notes the two distinct layers of scale, millions of devices profiled as preliminary reconnaissance versus the at least 45 infected, and the sensitive networks where impressions appeared including defence ministries armed forces national cyber agencies intergovernmental and multilateral security organisations such as NATO and critical infrastructure as reported by Citizen Lab, with Confiant's data adding NATO the United Nations the European Parliament Sweden's Armed Forces Saab Intel and Nvidia, while preserving the report's careful qualification that an impression by itself does not constitute infection. Covers Confiant's finding that the ad code copied host websites' first-party cookies across more than a thousand publisher domains including logged-in session IDs and sometimes names and emails in tokens even without GDPR consent, and the observation that Discover-Tech leveraged GDPR consent frameworks to target EU users, arguing consent frameworks provided a compliance appearance rather than a constraint. Covers the six-year certification problem, with Discover-Tech appearing on Google and IAB Europe certified and approved vendor lists from 2020 to 2026 while serving ads through Google Yandex Vungle Beeswax Eskimi Sunteng and Xandr, and the report's sharpest general criticism that the industry uses certified and approved to convey a veneer of effective self-regulation while performing no meaningful due diligence and instead relying on self-attestation via an online form checkbox. Lists the recommendations for vendors (real-time detection and blocking, threat sharing, mandatory know-your-customer and recurring vetting, mandatory third-party audits of vendor registries, default-deny for problem jurisdictions, supply chain transparency) and for regulators (investigate Discover-Tech and Candiru, enforce existing law, use sanctions and entity-listing powers, commission investigations into advertising ecosystem risk, remove personal data from RTB auctions, and genuinely regulate the industry). Closes by arguing the novelty is not the absence of interaction but that zero-click exploitation found a global per-identity channel that looks like background rather than anomaly, that the two-stage design generalises to any defence checking what content appears to be rather than what it will do, that the anomalous business model is a more detectable signal than anomalous content, that the report's precise boundaries should be preserved (no attribution to a specific government, impressions on sensitive networks are not proven infections), and that because the channel's value and its risk come from the same design property the real fix requires accepting a loss of capability.
  - Key topics: AdFection, Citizen Lab, report 195, Discover-Tech, Candiru, Integrity Labs, Bindecy, Intelos, DARK CARTOGRAPHER, Confiant, zero-click spyware, targeted advertising, malvertising, real-time bidding, RTB, DSP, SSP, ad exchange, ad tag, tracking pixel, SDK, NOAS server, getAd server, 0-byte response, script tag, JavaScript exploit, browser exploit, fingerprinting, de-anonymization, ADINT, advertising intelligence, Controlium, MyDSP, Banner Tester, mobile advertising ID, cookie ID, IP address, ID syncing, cookie syncing, urlscan, Censys, Fingerprint V1, Fingerprint C1, COM hijack, 48-byte XOR, validator server, command and control, Al Jazeera, SHA256, VirusTotal, GDPR consent framework, first-party cookies, session IDs, Beeswax, FreeWheel, Comcast, Google, IAB Europe, Yandex, Vungle, Liftoff, Eskimi, Sunteng, Xandr, vendor registry, certified vendor, self-attestation, know-your-customer, third-party audit, entity listing, sanctions, Dekel Boni, Eric Banoun, Sara Hamou, Intellexa, NSO Group, Circles, Senpai Technologies, NATO, European Parliament, International Atomic Energy Agency, Al Jazeera, Duolingo, Viber, Truecaller, Yahoo Mail, CBC, New York Times, BBC, Haaretz, 译文


- [npm 拿「名字」而不是「ID」验证发布者：SlugFest 让 1500 个包的发布权可以被继承](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-10-13_npm-trusted-publishing-slugfest/): Translation+analysis of Bloom Security's disclosure (reported by CSO Online, 13 October 2026) of a flaw in npm's Trusted Publishing mechanism codenamed SlugFest. Explains the mechanism first: Trusted Publishing lets maintainers publish through OIDC from automated workflows so there are no long-lived credentials, and npm's documentation says a configuration's first successful publish validates it and binds it to the repository's immutable identity, but the trust configuration relied on the GitHub repository's human-readable owner/name rather than its permanent numeric ID. Because a repository can be renamed, transferred or deleted and its former name then claimed by someone else, an attacker could create a repository at that address with a workflow file matching the expected name and obtain a valid publishing credential for a package they do not own, without compromising the legitimate maintainer's GitHub or npm account or stealing any credential. Notes that the researchers demonstrated this against a package they controlled, publishing a new version from a GitHub repository belonging to a different organisation, and that their registry-wide scan found more than 1,500 potentially vulnerable packages with over 10 million combined downloads, more than one million monthly downloads, one package exceeding 200,000 monthly downloads, and a set that includes security scanners, authentication tools and cryptographic libraries - an irony given that components meant to protect other software are themselves supply-chain exposed. Argues the root cause is a generalisable failure mode of substituting a mutable, reclaimable identifier for an immutable identity, so the attacker no longer targets who you are but what you used to be called, and places it alongside domain expiry and re-registration, typosquatting and subdomain takeover, where the common property is that the identifier's lifetime is shorter than the trust relationship's. Compares name-based versus ID-based verification across readability, implementation cost, behaviour on rename and attack surface, concluding that in a supply-chain context readability does not justify inheritable trust. Covers the fix announced by GitHub on 2 October 2026 (unvalidated Trusted Publishing configurations expire 48 hours after creation and can no longer authorise publishing, a configuration becomes validated and exempt after its first successful publish, changing repository or project identity requires a new trust relationship with a fresh 48-hour window while ordinary edits do not restart the deadline, and expired configurations remain visible without counting toward per-package limits) plus the same-day tightening that npm now rejects trusted publishing tokens from GitHub Actions issue_comment events alongside the existing pull_request_target restriction, recommending push, release or workflow_dispatch instead. Praises the 48-hour window for precisely removing the dangerous state of a long-lived unvalidated trust configuration without imposing an immediate-publish requirement, and notes the detail that ordinary edits do not restart the window as evidence of thinking about bypasses. Notes that Bloom withheld the affected package names so users cannot check against a list and can only verify that a package's provenance attestation names the repository the project should come from, and that npm's GitLab trusted publishing integration has the same weakness. Then covers why AI coding agents amplify the consequences with measured figures from dozens of organisations (roughly 70 agent-installed packages per endpoint per month rising to about 350 on developer machines, direct installations only excluding transitive dependencies), the description that agents resolve dependencies themselves, tend to take the latest version and rarely check where a package came from, and the quotable line that a hijacked package no longer needs to find a developer, only to be the package an agent chooses; contrasts the traditional path where a human decides, may look at the repository and remembers what was added against the agent path where the dependency solver picks a version and the tree changes without notice. Also notes related industry context (npm v12 planned to block install scripts, Git dependencies and remote sources by default, described as the registry's most significant trust redesign) and the structural observation that OIDC trusted publishing verifies who built a package rather than what code was in the repository when it was built. Closes with concrete maintainer actions (npm trust list, confirm each trusted repository still resolves to a repository you control, delete and recreate bindings pointing at renamed or transferred repositories, remove the binding before deleting a repository, move publishing to permitted events, and the official recommendation to require two-factor authentication and disallow tokens) and, for consumers, the honest limitation that without a published list only provenance verification and controlling what gets installed are available, with the recommendation that teams using AI agents make dependency installation policy explicit and keep dependency changes visible in review.
  - Key topics: npm, Trusted Publishing, SlugFest, Bloom Security, Golan Myers, OIDC, GitHub Actions, provenance attestation, immutable repository ID, slug, repository rename, repository transfer, repository delete, name reclaim, supply chain attack, T1195.002, 48-hour expiry, issue_comment, pull_request_target, push event, workflow_dispatch, require 2FA and disallow tokens, npm trust list, GitLab trusted publishing, AI coding agents, agent-installed packages, transitive dependencies, npm v12, install scripts, 译文

- [内网域名没有一个是安全的：.lan / .local / .home / .corp 的真实状态，以及 ICANN 给出的 .internal](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-10-14_internal-tld-name-collision/): Original research on the real status of private-network domain names, verified against the IANA Special-Use Domain Names Registry and live root-server queries. Establishes that the IANA registry (per RFC 6761) contains only two names intended for internal use: home.arpa (RFC 8375) and local (RFC 6762); .lan, .corp, .home, .internal and .private are all unregistered, with only home.arpa and local carrying IETF references. Explains what unregistered means by querying the root servers directly (dig lan|corp|home|internal NS @198.41.0.4 all return NXDOMAIN, with the aa Authoritative Answer flag set, confirming a deliberate authoritative denial rather than an error; arpa is the sole exception with a real NS record), and why malformed queries such as printer.lan.lan appear in internal DNS logs as clients keep appending suffixes and walking the devolution chain up to the root. Then dissects each name. .local is standardised by RFC 6762 but is reserved as link-local with meaning only on the originating link, so queries must go to the mDNS multicast addresses 224.0.0.251 and FF02::FB rather than unicast DNS; configuring it as an ordinary DNS zone is a misuse that causes intermittent resolution failures because mDNS and traditional DNS answer the same name in competition. home.arpa is the only ordinary-DNS residential domain with an RFC, and RFC 8375 states plainly why .home was abandoned: IETF does not administer the root zone, so it cannot prevent .home from being delegated to a commercial registry, and .arpa is managed by IETF itself so it can never be commercialised. .lan is the most widely used but has zero protection, discussed in ICANN's public comment period yet not selected. .corp, .home and .mail have had delegation explicitly halted because internal enterprise use was so heavy that delegation would cause a global simultaneous collision, but this is a policy decision rather than a technical guarantee. .internal is the official answer: recommended by SSAC-113 in September 2020, reserved by ICANN Board resolution in July 2024, and drafted as draft-davies-internal-tld by authors from IANA, ICANN and Google, whose text requires it MUST NOT appear in the DNS root zone, explicitly to steer operators away from .corp, .home and .lan. Covers three concrete risk scenarios (query leakage to the public root, name collision enabling man-in-the-middle attacks as described in US-CERT TA16-144A with Verisign measuring roughly 20 million vulnerable queries per day, and certificate-authority conflicts) plus the Microsoft Active Directory recommendation to use a subdomain of a domain you actually own such as ad.example.com rather than .corp, .local or .lan. Recommends home.arpa for home networks and your own domain's subdomain for enterprises, and argues that for existing .lan/.corp/.home deployments the first step is isolation rather than migration: setting the zone to local-zone: "lan." static in unbound makes the server authoritative for the whole tree so undefined names return a local NXDOMAIN with the aa flag and never reach upstream, cutting off both the leakage and the hijacking path in one change.
  - Key topics: DNS, internal naming, name collision, ICANN, IANA, Special-Use Domain Names, RFC 6761, RFC 8375, RFC 6762, home.arpa, .internal, .lan, .corp, .home, .mail, .private, .local, mDNS, Multicast DNS, Avahi, NXDOMAIN, authoritative answer, DNS devolution, DNS search list, root zone delegation, SSAC-113, draft-davies-internal-tld, new gTLD program, US-CERT TA16-144A, Verisign, man-in-the-middle, Active Directory, Kerberos, LDAP, unbound, dnsmasq, local-zone static, 原创

- [Intel 让 SGX 在 Diamond Rapids 之后退场：这不是失败，是「边界选错了」](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-10-12_intel-sgx-phaseout-tdx-pivot/): Translation+analysis of Intel's newsroom post (by Mike Ferron-Jones, go-to-market lead for platform security and integrity) announcing that the next-generation Xeon platform codenamed Diamond Rapids will be the last to include Intel SGX, with the confidential computing roadmap refocused on Intel TDX, read alongside Tom's Hardware and other coverage. Quotes Intel's stated reason verbatim, that SGX established confidential computing in the data centre and continues to serve security-conscious customers but the industry has increasingly coalesced around virtual machine isolation technologies like TDX because they offer the scalability, ease of deployment and operational model customers need for broad adoption, and notes the wording carefully: it does not claim SGX is insecure, it says the industry chose something else. Explains the architectural distinction in a table: SGX protects an application enclave with the smallest trust boundary but usually requiring application modification, while TDX protects an entire virtual machine (trust domain) with a larger boundary where applications typically need no changes and existing VM operations apply, with the hypervisor and cloud administrators outside the boundary and the guest OS inside it. Argues industry convergence (AMD SEV-SNP and ARM CCA follow the same per-VM or per-realm isolation path) and that the three stated reasons each correspond to a concrete friction, concluding that protection strength and breadth of adoption are independent dimensions where adoption often decides the final value. Covers the transition arrangement as the best-handled part of the announcement (support and security updates for platforms with SGX continuing into the early 2030s, several years for customers to plan, validate and migrate at their own pace, and language that does not disparage existing deployments), while noting that continued support does not imply new features. Then covers the AI-agent framing Intel uses to justify the pivot, quoting its argument that trust becomes as important as intelligence as agents move into production and organisations need trusted infrastructure to verify what agents are, what they can access, how they operate, and that their execution has not been compromised, and noting this asks who can see data at the moment it is processed rather than how it is protected at rest and in transit. Lists the deployment evidence (Apple's Private Cloud Compute expanded with Google Cloud using Intel TDX trust domains on Xeon, and OPPO's comparable Private Computing Cloud described as sensitive data always usable but never visible), cloud availability (Microsoft Azure, Alibaba Cloud, Google Cloud, IBM Cloud and Volcano Cloud), enterprise platform support (Red Hat, Canonical, VMware) alongside Intel's own point that security technologies are most valuable when they can be deployed broadly and consistently without modifying every application, and the need to coordinate confidential computing across CPU and GPU with NVIDIA so protection does not break when data reaches GPU memory. Details the three planned TDX enhancements and what each addresses (trusted I/O with TDX Connect for confidential VM to PCIe device communication, post-quantum cryptography, and enhanced attestation) plus the four simultaneous conditions TDX Connect requires, explains that data inside a confidential VM is decrypted inside the CPU so protection comes from hardware isolation and the chain is only as strong as its weakest link, and closes by arguing the pivot reflects market rejection of a boundary choice rather than a technology failure, that the transition handling is exemplary for a hardware security feature subject to long compliance cycles, and that a confidential VM does not protect against your own application's bugs since it addresses untrusted infrastructure rather than untrusted code.
  - Key topics: Intel, Intel SGX, Intel TDX, Diamond Rapids, confidential computing, trusted execution environment, enclave, trust domain, VM isolation, application isolation, trust boundary, remote attestation, Intel TDX Connect, trusted I/O, TDISP, PCIe gen 6, post-quantum cryptography, AMD SEV-SNP, ARM CCA, agentic AI, AI agents, data sovereignty, Apple Private Cloud Compute, OPPO, Microsoft Azure, Alibaba Cloud, Google Cloud, IBM Cloud, Volcano Cloud, Red Hat, Canonical, VMware, NVIDIA, Xeon 6, 译文

- [数据中心挨打这件事，现在能在互联网测量数据里读出来](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-10-12_yandex-data-centers-bot-traffic-collapse/): Translation+analysis of Tom's Hardware's report on the effects of successive strikes on Yandex data centres, explicitly avoiding politics and treating only the measurable internet-infrastructure data. Lays out the timeline and the numbers: Cloudflare reporting that bot traffic from the Yandex network fell to 0.4 percent of the maximum HTTP request volume recorded over the preceding two weeks, with an earlier drop to about 57 percent on 8 October when a Yandex data centre in Sasovo housing two supercomputers was hit; a second larger campus in Kaluga knocked offline; a third attack the night before publication; NetBlocks measuring Yandex Cloud traffic at 30 percent and Yandex LLC at 63 percent; and the Yandex Cloud status page showing at least 84 services offline. Also covers the resilience context (Starlink does not work in Russia and the competing Rassvet constellation has seen a number of satellites fall back to the ground after launch, so ordinary users have no high-speed satellite backup) and the precedent that AWS sites in Bahrain and the UAE have been hit multiple times since the US bombing campaign against Iran began, with AWS telling customers to move data outside the region and offering no recovery timeline. Argues that the technically interesting part is the measurement capability rather than the strikes themselves, breaking down what each observer can see (Cloudflare measuring bot traffic from a network against recent peaks at near real time, NetBlocks measuring overall traffic levels of an autonomous system or cloud service as a percentage of normal, and the affected party's own status page giving service-level counts) and noting the underlying techniques (BGP and traffic sampling, external DNS and HTTP probes, and public status telemetry cross-validating each other). Identifies two resulting capabilities: external assessment of attack effects, which makes effectiveness claims checkable and measurable by third parties, and immediate visibility of third-party dependency risk, since region-level single points of failure become observable historical events that should push multi-region design. Then flags a reading trap: the headline claim that Russian disinformation bot traffic was eliminated in a night overreaches, because the measurement is of bot traffic from the Yandex network, which is a combined search, mail and cloud network rather than a single propaganda platform; capacity can be rebuilt elsewhere at far lower cost than physical infrastructure; and the category of bot traffic includes legitimate automation such as crawlers and monitoring, so traffic reaching zero is not the same as capability reaching zero. Notes the report's account of both sides' stated justifications without evaluating them, observes that data centres are becoming targets that are critical yet not treated like protected civilian infrastructure while carrying functions overlapping with civilian services, and draws the practical lesson that a region-level failure can last for days with no stated recovery timeline, so disaster recovery objectives should be self-sustaining rather than waiting for someone else to recover first.

- [「我们可能会失去公钥密码学」：Green 那条推文背后到底在说什么](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-10-09_green-public-key-cryptography-ai/): Full translation of the 15-tweet clarification thread Matthew Green (Johns Hopkins) posted on 8 October 2026 after a casual reply tweet of his ('I think we might lose public key cryptography', clarified as 'well, encryption specifically') was widely reshared. Covers his opening warning against overreaction (don't stop using TLS, don't post Bitcoin seeds in cleartext, don't start treating Telegram as a secure messenger - 'encryption is good, use it'), his explicit statement that he knows of no imminent cryptanalysis results and his inference from the questions being asked about which frontier labs probably do not have one, and the precise scope of his concern: not public-key cryptography in principle and not all of it, but standardized public-key encryption and some signatures, specifically because most of it rests on a small number of hard problems - currently essentially MLWE and ECDLP, with LWE and syndrome decoding as backups. Sets out his central argument: these problems were extensively analysed by humans and we felt confident that the best known attacks were the best attacks, but we are learning that human mathematical analysis is not the gold standard; the optimistic view that we got it all right is 'a very opinionated bet', and opinionated bets are not safe when global Internet security is at stake. Explains what losing public-key encryption would mean - not that encryption becomes impossible or that we live in Minicrypt, but that new cryptanalytic results substantially improve attacks on standardized schemes, with the milder effect being that schemes thought to offer 128-bit security are really 96 or 108 bits, forcing honest standards bodies to deprecate at least the smaller parameter sets already deployed in live systems. Then the crux: crank parameters up to what, when current numbers rest on 40 (or 25) years of human study and we could be off by 26 bits; the fallback would be trusting that the machines say they are stuck, which he says nobody will feel good about, especially if a new internal model makes another step-change jump, leaving trust only at painfully high security levels. Adds the trigger context the Chinese discussion omits: OpenAI's release of 722 AI-generated mathematical papers (grouped into about 372, roughly 4,000 problems fed in, about 5 percent success rate) that Scott Aaronson called the 'Mathocalypse', three papers withdrawn on 7 October over a sign error in a Weil-classes proof, and criticism from Terence Tao and the Association for Human Mathematicians. Covers the industry reaction (Ethereum researcher Justin Drake urging 'bunker mode' preparation, Vitalik Buterin arguing AI may threaten cryptocurrency more than quantum computers and that lattices will need to be significantly bigger, plus his advice to hold funds in addresses whose public keys have not yet been exposed) and the crucial caveat that no evidence shows OpenAI's results come close to defeating deployed cryptography, and that the correctness of the proofs is itself unverified. Closes by noting his prior posts (July on Anthropic's Claude Mythos attack on HAWK reducing effective key recovery from 2^64 to 2^38 and improved reduced-round AES attacks, and August on software going 'dark'), and by separating technical risk from the epistemic risk that we lose the ability to know how safe we are.
  - Key topics: Matthew Green, public key cryptography, MLWE, ECDLP, LWE, syndrome decoding, lattice cryptography, parameter sizes, 128-bit security level, standards bodies, deprecation, Minicrypt, Impagliazzo, NIST, HAWK, Claude Mythos, Anthropic, OpenAI 722 math papers, Mathocalypse, Scott Aaronson, Terence Tao, Association for Human Mathematicians, Vitalik Buterin, Justin Drake, bunker mode, quantum computers, post-quantum migration, epistemic risk, Telegram, TLS, Bitcoin seed phrases, 译文

- [Google 开放 SynthID 检测器：它的价值不在「能不能识破 AI」，而在「阳性意味着什么」](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-10-09_google-synthid-detector-public/): Translation+analysis of TechRepublic's coverage of Google opening the SynthID Detector to the public in English, letting anyone upload media to check whether it carries an invisible AI watermark. Covers the mechanism (it does not assess whether a file 'looks' AI-generated but searches for the invisible mark embedded by supported AI systems), the scale (more than 180 billion images and videos watermarked, plus 240,000 years of audio), format support (11 image, three video and six audio formats including JPG, PNG, WEBP, GIF, MP4, MOV, MP3, WAV and FLAC), participation from other vendors' watermarking (OpenAI, NVIDIA and Kakao, with Apple expected soon), and existing integration in Gemini, Search and Chrome handling over one million verification requests daily, which makes the website a consolidated entry point for an existing system rather than new technology. Sets out the limitations the coverage states: it cannot identify every piece of AI-generated content because companies use different watermarking systems and some models use none at all, open-weight models can generate unwatermarked content, watermarks may in some circumstances be removed, and the tool cannot distinguish a wholly AI-created file from one merely edited by AI, so a positive result establishes that supported AI was involved but not exactly how. Notes the roughly 10 checks per user per day limit and that its purpose is to make it harder to repeatedly test similar files while developing ways to remove SynthID, which amounts to an admission that watermarks can be attacked and that the response is raising the cost. Adds the academic layer the original omits: SynthID-Text is vulnerable to meaning-preserving attacks including paraphrasing, copy-paste modification and back-translation, with simple character perturbation or short-form paraphrasing sufficient to evade detection; dilution attacks embed a watermarked passage inside a larger unwatermarked body to weaken the whole-text signal; C2PA's metadata manifest route is vulnerable because metadata is often stripped accidentally and can be trivially removed; and cross-layer contradictions can be manufactured, with an AI-generated image passed through a C2PA-compliant editor producing a valid provenance manifest asserting only a human editing action while still carrying a synthetic-content watermark - though the research also confirms watermarks remain persistent enough under standard editorial workflows to produce detectable cross-layer inconsistencies. Closes with the governance critique from 'Watermarking Without Standards Is Not AI Governance' (no standardized robustness evaluation protocol across modalities, and the structural dilemma that open-source detectors can be exploited either to evade detection or to forge apparently watermarked content), and three practical rules: treat a negative result as no information rather than clearance, remember that a positive only indicates involvement and not extent, and cross-check watermark against metadata with inconsistency itself treated as a red flag.
  - Key topics: SynthID, SynthID Detector, AI watermarking, content provenance, C2PA, content credentials, invisible watermark, Google DeepMind, Gemini, Search, Chrome, OpenAI, NVIDIA, Kakao, Apple, open-weight models, watermark removal, adversarial robustness, paraphrasing, back-translation, dilution attack, metadata stripping, cross-layer inconsistency, watermark forgery, AI governance, false positive, false negative, 原创

- [54% 掉到 22%：抗量子准备度这个指标，量错了层](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-10-09_pqc-edge-quantum-readiness/): Translation+analysis of CSO Online's coverage of F5 Labs' 2026 State of PQC on the Web study, which found that 54 percent of the world's top one million websites now support post-quantum key exchange - a figure F5 Labs director David Warburton immediately qualifies, noting most of that comes from CDN providers enabling PQC by default and that removing Cloudflare-hosted sites drops it to 22 percent. Covers the measurement gap in detail: F5 examined only website front ends without accessing application servers behind the CDN (Akamai, Cloudflare, Amazon CloudFront) and without determining whether internal traffic uses PQC, which Warburton says could be an even bigger harvest-now-decrypt-later target - everything behind what CDNs switch on, the hop to origin, service meshes, VPNs, SSH and code signing, is invisible from outside and that is where enterprise readiness actually lives. Sets out the supporting figures (only 35 percent of government and telecom websites support PQ key exchange, more than one in ten sites in the wider sample still lack TLS 1.3, and just 27 percent of CISOs are actively implementing PQC per a June KPMG survey while 38 percent consider quantum a top high-impact emerging threat), then the expert assessments from Deloitte (CDN-enabled PQC protects the client-to-edge connection but does not automatically extend to origin servers, internal APIs, service-to-service communications or enterprise PKI; planning maturity must not be confused with deployment maturity, and HSM, payment infrastructure, PKI and third-party dependencies block financial institutions while long-lived OT and constrained devices do the same in industrial settings), PQShield (NIST finalised its first PQC standards in 2024 but the IETF only published the hybrid post-quantum key exchange standard for TLS 1.3 in August 2026) and Keyfactor (F5's figures reflect a web focus rather than organisational initiative, with financial services, telecom, government and a rapidly accelerating healthcare sector leading). Details the hard constraints: the 54 percent measures key exchange support while PQC certificates are not yet available for the public internet, so Merkle Tree Certificates will help desktop and mobile browsers but many other environments need PQC certificates and their much larger size will cause problems; and the looming 47-day certificate lifetime enforcement, where Warburton warns anyone still provisioning certificates manually will face serious challenges. Covers the technical debt sources (legacy clients, partner integrations and change-control processes; vendors that have not yet updated products for PQC; and the confusion of migration roadmaps with deployment) and the industry-accepted remedy path: inventory cryptographic usage, prioritise data that must stay confidential for years, plan upgrades for the systems that take longest to change, look beyond the public website to internal applications, APIs, VPNs, identity systems and embedded libraries, build a cryptographic bill of materials with a named owner keeping it current, remove legacy dependencies, enable hybrid PQC where possible and automate certificate management. Adds a supplementary regulatory timeline with sources: NIST IR 8547 (draft November 2024) proposing RSA-2048 and ECC P-256 class algorithms be deprecated after 2030 and disallowed after 2035, NSA's CNSA 2.0 track completing by 2033, and the US executive directive setting key establishment for federal high-value assets by the end of 2030 and digital signatures by the end of 2031 - noting NIST considers AES-256 already quantum-resistant and that ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA can and should be deployed now. Closes with practitioner-tier advice: start inventory with SSH host keys and code signing rather than websites because those keys outlive TLS certificates and sit squarely in the harvest-now-decrypt-later window, treat certificate automation as valuable independent of quantum readiness, and schedule 'PQC key exchange' and 'PQC certificates' as separate projects.

- [微软把「跑不可信代码」做成了一个 SDK 依赖：九个沙箱后端与一份说清边界的文档](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-10-09_microsoft-mxc-sandbox-sdk/): Analysis of Microsoft's open-sourced MXC (Microsoft eXecution Container), a sandboxed code execution system for running untrusted code (model output, plugins, tools) on Windows, Linux and macOS, shipped as an SDK dependency embedded in the consuming application rather than a service to operate. Covers the positioning (the app specifies container type, containment rules and the workload command; MXC validates, selects a backend and launches), the three versioned SDKs (Rust mxc-sdk on crates.io, .NET Microsoft.Mxc.Sdk on NuGet, Node @microsoft/mxc-sdk on npm, all behind v1 namespaces with the Node package root exporting no APIs), the standalone executors (wxc-exec.exe, lxc-exec, mxc-exec-mac) and the stable 1.0.0 vs dev 1.1.0-alpha schemas. Explains the policy model: filesystem read-only/read-write/denied paths, directional network contracts with independent egress/ingress defaults where any omission resolves to deny, hostLoopback requested separately from ingress.default, direct CIDR rules and runtimeConfig.networkProxy being mutually exclusive, and pre-0.9.0-alpha fields being rejected outright ('changing only the version is not a migration'). Details the Windows ProcessContainer enforcement (per-container SID-scoped WFP egress filters where explicit blocks win, plus a per-container WinHTTP proxy with HTTP_PROXY/HTTPS_PROXY set; the AppContainer four-quadrant capability matrix and its bidirectional privateNetworkClientServer limitation) and all nine backends across three platforms, including bubblewrap as the stable Linux default requiring bwrap 0.5.0+ (--ro-bind-try, --clearenv), macOS Seatbelt applied via sandbox_init() between fork() and exec() with the profile passed as a string, and the experimental hardware-virtualisation tier (Nanvix microVM at ~100 ms cold start and ~100 MB resident, Hyperlight booting a Unikraft unikernel from a warm snapshot, Windows Sandbox VMs). Highlights where the documentation states its own limits rather than hiding them: bubblewrap rejecting enforceable-looking requests it cannot honour before provisioning, the identity-less host proxy labelled a weaker development/testing deployment, AppContainer compatibility explicitly not equivalent to the WFP guarantees, one-shot VM teardown being best-effort rather than kernel-guaranteed, platform probes caching successes but not failures (and execution re-probing so a changed PATH target cannot reuse a stale result), and --audit disabling all sandbox security for the analysed workload with a warning never to run untrusted code under it. Also covers the telemetry design (Windows-only, off unless the run opts in and the user consents and administrative policy permits, HKLM policy as 'a ceiling, never a grant' with HKCU deliberately not honoured, and local open-source builds not routing telemetry to Microsoft). Closes with four takeaways: a unified isolation abstraction must carry rejection semantics, defaults are the product, capability differences must be stated rather than inferred, and debugging affordances are the easiest place for a security hole to appear.
  - Key topics: Microsoft MXC, Microsoft eXecution Container, sandbox, isolated code execution, untrusted code, agent sandboxing, bubblewrap, bwrap, Seatbelt, AppContainer, WFP, WinHTTP, Windows Sandbox, LXC, Nanvix, microVM, Hyperlight, Unikraft, WSLC, IsolationSession, deny by default, egress ingress policy, hostLoopback, JSON schema versioning, rejection semantics, telemetry policy, MIT license, 译文

- [钓鱼防御打错了层级：域名封不过来，但服务器藏不住](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-10-09_phishing-server-layer-aitm/): Combined translation+analysis of two articles: Yanky Wilson's CSO Online piece 'We are fighting phishing at the wrong layer' and Google's 'Chrome's Response to Recent ccTLD Registry Hijacks'. From the first: the attacker economics (registering a domain to serving a live credential-harvesting page in under 24 minutes, of which 12 were nameserver propagation, replacement cost about one dollar), why modern kits are adversary-in-the-middle proxies that relay the real Microsoft sign-in and harvest credentials plus session tokens (a single 2022 Microsoft-documented campaign reached over 10,000 organizations, and per Obsidian Security the large majority of accounts compromised through such kits already had MFA enabled), the finding that a null result from internet-wide scanners against a hostname-gated origin means you knocked in the wrong language rather than nothing being there, the pivot mechanism (the proxy relays upstream response headers unmodified, so the victim's browser stores a cookie set by Microsoft recording the proxy's own source IP — the proxy writes its return address on the envelope and hands it to the person it is robbing), the methodology discipline (attempting to falsify the finding for an hour, requiring independent corroboration before writing the word origin, publishing unproven results as unproven), the resulting estate map (one reported phishing email led via passive DNS to a second dormant domain, a unique registrar, a handful of shared machines, and two servers carrying domains from separate cloud identity tenants the operator kept apart — dozens of lookalike domains impersonating manufacturers, staffing agencies and waste haulers built over six months for invoice fraud), and the tenant-side detection inversion (the successful sign-in your tenant records carries the relay's address, not the employee's; hunt in hosting/VPS ranges, and remember tokens persist so attacker activity surfaces as refresh-token events rather than fresh interactive sign-ins; revoke sessions before resetting credentials, never the reverse). From the second: third-party hijacks of the .gh, .sl and .as ccTLD registries, where attackers modified authoritative DNS and obtained unauthorized HTTPS certificates covering Google and other organizations' domains, Chrome's response (CRLSets blocking, CA revocation coordination, CT-log analysis proactively identifying and blocking certificates of additional impacted brands), Google's explicit caveat that browser-side intervention should not be relied on, and the two domain-owner actions: monitor CT logs across the entire domain portfolio including parked and regional ccTLD properties, and publish restrictive CAA records with ACME account bindings (RFC 8657) because CAs may cache and reuse completed DCV checks, letting an attacker mint new certificates after a hijack ends. Closes with the structural mismatch table: defenders spend effort on the adversary's cheapest layer while shared hosting infrastructure quietly defeats compartmentalized identity.

- [16 岁少年用 AI 助手攻破微软内部分析库：170 亿行数据、JWT 不验签，赏金 5000 美元](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-09-28_microsoft-titan-analytics-jwt-flaw/): Translation+analysis of Tom's Hardware (2026-09-28) plus Rescana's technical post and the researcher's blog (blog.faav.net). A **16-year-old researcher "Faav"**, using a custom **AI hacking assistant "Antares"**, found that Microsoft's **internal Titan Analytics** service (Azure-hosted, exposed a public API documented via Swagger) **did not cryptographically verify JWT signatures** — it only checked claims (tenant ID, audience, app ID, user identity) and **accepted `alg: none` tokens with empty signatures**. Crafting an `alg: none` JWT with the `upn` claim set to `admin` mapped to **local user ID 1** (admin-reserved), granting full admin access and **arbitrary SQL queries against ClickHouse** — potentially exposing **~17.3 trillion rows** across **17 ClickHouse databases, 9,863 tables, 30 active API routes** and **~25,000 user accounts**. Timeline: discovered **2026-08-25**, reported to MSRC **2026-09-05 (case 144051)**, endpoint locked down **2026-09-09**; **$5,000** bounty. Scope: **internal service only — all builds/deployments up to 2026-09-09; not present in any commercial/customer-facing product**. MITRE ATT&CK: T1078, T1552, T1190, T1606. IoC: abnormal `/v2/Query` access from non-internal IPs; backend accepting `alg:none`/empty signatures. Takeaways: `alg:none` / "trust claims not signatures" is a textbook anti-pattern that still recurs in big-vendor internal services ("internal network = trusted" downgrade); AI assistance lowers the discovery bar (parallels the Hacktron/DeepSeek/Enclave "attack cost collapse" line); internal ≠ safe (public-documented endpoints + weaker review); defenses: enforce JWT signature verification, reject `alg:none`/empty signatures, restrict accepted algorithms, inventory internal API exposure, monitor query routes for non-internal sources. Source boundary: TH returned only title/lede on fetch; technical detail from Rescana + researcher blog, labeled as such.
