- [文件通知攻击：Linux / Windows / macOS 的文件监控子系统正在泄漏你的操作](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-09-24_file-notification-attacks-sidechannel/): Translation+analysis of a Graz University of Technology paper (Sudheendra Raghav Neela et al., CCS '26, 2026-09-18 preprint; project page inoti.fyi) — the first generic **file-notification template attacks** on Linux, Windows and macOS. Modern OSes ship filesystem-event subsystems — Linux **inotify**, Windows **ReadDirectoryChangesW**, macOS **FSEvents** — that let any process with read access subscribe to file events (access/write/open/close), but the attack surface was poorly understood (prior work only showed Android app-start leakage). Two phases: an offline, semi-automated **templating** phase finds cause-effect leakage between user activity and file events (terminal commands, keyboard/mouse input, browsing, web-server activity, printing, VMs and containers, Bluetooth/network/VPN changes, USB interaction), then an **attack** phase spies with it — ≤0.21% CPU overhead, **0.2–11.5 ms** temporal resolution. Results: **Linux** — local and remote (SSH) inter-keystroke timing F1 **93.1%–100%** across 7 users (66% of keys within 1 ms), a real authentication UI-redress attack on KDE Plasma 6 (Wayland), and top-100 website fingerprinting at **87.9%** F1 open-world; **Android** — a novel unprivileged primitive reveals the existence of permission-protected files apps can't access (e.g. WhatsApp); **Windows** — any unprivileged user leaks the **full paths of all files even without read permission** on a directory (e.g. user home dirs), giving direct file-usage leakage and top-1000 website fingerprinting at **97.8%** F1 in one pass; **macOS** — least leakage, still enough to monitor specific app starts/interactions. Root cause: unprivileged users can use the notification subsystem, and on **both** Windows and Linux (independent implementations) an attacker can get events for files it **cannot read**; file existence and filenames alone leak a lot. Key Linux detail — the **Unreadable File Bypass**: if the parent directory is world-readable (/var/log, /dev), an unprivileged user can watch the *directory* and receive events for all files inside, including unreadable ones (syslog); a test machine's **/dev** had **278 unreadable files** that still trigger notifications. Concretely: **/dev/input** gives inter-keystroke timing (two notifications per key: down/up; access patterns distinguish dense touchpad bursts from sporadic keyboard presses), /dev/snd, /dev/bus/usb and /dev/tun leak audio-setting interaction, USB plug-ins and VPN activation, and **/usr/share** leaks the most (KDE search fires events per keystroke in searchproviders; Firefox browsing different sites touches **different font files** under /usr/share/fonts → website fingerprinting). Disclosure: responsibly reported Oct 2025 to Linux/Windows/macOS/KDE; all acknowledged; **Linux deployed partial patches**; **Microsoft called the privacy-compromising undocumented behavior *by-design***, arguing it "only reveals file names and paths within another user's profile directory [and] does not expose file contents." Mitigations: better fine-grained user permission models and stronger file-notification APIs. Takeaways: (1) filename + timing as a side channel is counter-intuitive and potent, needing **no special hardware** (hardware-agnostic), only OS-provided APIs; (2) the Linux leakage points expose the overlooked "world-readable directory" design surface — *directory readable ≠ contents safe*; (3) Windows' by-design response is a **structural** risk, not a missing patch — when metadata leakage is ruled by-design there's no CVE/patch/upgrade nudge, turning a fixable bug into an architectural fact; (4) mitigation lifts the problem from ops to OS architecture; (5) on multi-user Linux/Windows hosts a low-privilege account can passively watch keystroke timing, browsing and container activity — single-user desktops are less exposed, but a compromised low-privilege service (systemd unprivileged services, XZ Utils) becomes an intel source.
  - Key topics: side channel, file notification, inotify, FSEvents, ReadDirectoryChangesW, OS security, inter-keystroke timing, website fingerprinting, template attack, privacy, Unreadable File Bypass, /dev/input, /usr/share, KDE Plasma, Windows by-design, Graz University of Technology, CCS 2026
- [WordPress 修补一个严重级漏洞：未认证 RCE，补丁发布数小时内即被利用](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-09-24_wordpress-critical-rce-cve-2026-87902/): Translation+analysis of Computerworld (Evan Schuman, 2026-09-24; originally CSOonline). WordPress patched a **critical-severity** hole, **CVE-2026-87902**, allowing an **unauthenticated attacker full remote code execution (RCE)**; in-the-wild attacks already reported, found by Swiss researcher Robert Ressl. WordPress 7.1.2 advisory: an unauthenticated attacker can, under certain conditions, make page-template resolution include a chosen readable local PHP file outside the active theme directories — and if the server-environment and active-theme preconditions are met, that leads to RCE; fix backported to 4.7, affecting **4.7.0–7.1.1** (~a decade of installs). Attack chain (Digital 520's Noah Kenney): the legitimate PHP package tool **`pearcmd.php`** is abused to write attacker content to disk — current attacks drop malicious PHP in `/tmp` then load it via the WordPress flaw, so a team watching only the WordPress directory misses stage one; once PHP executes, attackers read `wp-config.php`, lift DB creds and auth keys, create admins, alter payment/lead forms, redirect visitors, plant persistence. Three takeaways: (1) **the disclosure-to-exploit window has collapsed to zero** — IDC's Philip Harris (new risk reality; mean time to exploit can be *negative*), Patchstack (probing under 5 hours after 7.1.2 shipped, ~10x volume in a day, scanning→payload), Tribeca Softech's Aman Mahapatra (anchor isn't the 9.2 CVSS, it's the patch-to-exploit gap — first exploitation blocked 11:49 UTC the same day with payloads matching the patch's exact encoding; "attackers did not discover this bug, they read the fix" — publishing a patch is now publishing an exploit guide); (2) **automated updates are a dilemma** — CISOs nervous about patch automation (CrowdStrike), Ressl (enabling auto-update ≠ verifying it installed; rapid tested rollout with verification across all exposed installs incl. staging), Mahapatra (enterprises disable auto-updates for change control, so the most mature governance is most exposed; change control that can't distinguish an unauthenticated RCE from a routine plugin update protects the process, not the enterprise), Luthra (security releases become attacker roadmaps; internet-facing emergency patching needs hours-level response); (3) **the deep water is forgotten WordPress sites** — corporate WordPress often runs below the radar, authorized at the time but unknown to IT; risk sits in never-inventoried web estates (marketing microsites, campaign landing pages, regional sites, agency-built investor pages, acquired-company properties), 4.7.0–7.1.1 ≈ a decade of installs with forgotten sites on old branches; worst in finance, where surfaced instances are almost never the corporate site but marketing/subsidiary/expired-agency assets absent from the CMDB. Response: upgrade to 7.1.2 (confirm backport on old branches), hunt `pearcmd.php` abuse + `/tmp` webshells, assume compromise and rotate wp-config DB creds/auth salts, give internet-facing criticals an hours-level fast lane, verify the patch actually installed, and run an external attack-surface sweep for forgotten assets.
  - Key topics: WordPress, CVE-2026-87902, critical vulnerability, RCE, unauthenticated, pearcmd.php, page template resolution, wp-config.php, patch management, change control, mean time to exploit, Patchstack, IDC, CMDB, EASM, attack surface, finance sector, incident response

- [ICANN 收到 1,615 份新顶级域申请和约 3.67 亿美元：但 55% 的申请注定撞在别人身上](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-10-09_icann-2026-new-gtld-round/): Analysis of ICANN's 2026 new gTLD round following Reveal Day on 7 October 2026, combining Computerworld's reporting with statistics the author computed directly from ICANN's published contention-set CSV. Covers the scale: 1,615 applications from 481 applicants, a 227,000 USD evaluation fee per application (up from 185,000 USD in 2012, covering one primary string plus up to four variants), roughly 367 million USD in evaluation fees, and the 333 brand, 16 community, 15 self-identified geographic and 21 internationalized domain name applications, with 864 applications from North America, 506 from Europe, 218 from Asia/Australia/Pacific, 16 from Africa and 11 from Latin America and the Caribbean. Lists the major tech applicants: Meta with 21 strings (.aiglasses, .facebook, .instagram, .llama, .meta, .metaai, .metaverse, .muse, .superintelligence, .threads, .wearables, .whatsapp), OpenAI with 15 (.chatgpt, .openai, .asi, .codex, .deploy, .evals, .gpt, .mcp, .model, .oai, .skill, .voice), Amazon with 8, and Microsoft and Anthropic with 2 each (.msft/.copilot and .anthropic/.claude). Presents the contention analysis computed from ICANN's CSV: 263 contention sets covering 891 applications, or 55.2 percent of all applications, with the size distribution (114 sets of two, 64 of three, 32 of four, and single sets of 10, 11 and 13), led by .agent with 13 applicants including Google's Charleston Road Registry, Meta Registry Holdings and OPENAI OPCO, then .bit with 11, .api/.brand/.hub with 10 each, and .agi with 7. Explains why this matters more than in 2012: ICANN's auction RFP states that of 234 contention sets in 2012 only 16 went to auction with most settled privately, while the 2026 round prohibits all forms of private resolution including private auctions, and ICANN projected roughly 133 contention sets against the 263 actually published. Details the cost stacking (227,000 USD entry fee, ICANN auction where the winner pays the second-highest bid expected around autumn 2027, 25,000-100,000 USD annual RSP fees with all applicants required to use an evaluated RSP of which 28 exist, plus 30,000-100,000 USD in professional services) and the narrow exit windows: the string replacement deadline of 21 October 2026, String Confirmation Day on 17 November 2026, and the final ten days after that to withdraw for a 65 percent refund - leaving roughly 79,000 USD net loss. Uses the 2012 round as a historical baseline (1,930 applications, 1,241 delegated, 653 withdrawn, 32 terminated, and a note that delegation totals are not adjusted for later terminations) and nTLDData renewal figures where the median new gTLD keep rate is 68.45 percent against 73.23 percent for .com/.net/.org, alongside its observation that 683 monthly filings reported deleting more domains than the TLD ever held. Separates the .ai case as an unrepeatable accident: Anguilla's ccTLD was assigned by ISO 3166 with no link to artificial intelligence, yet earned EC$230M (about 85.3M USD) in 2025, roughly 47 percent of government revenue, with over one million registrations by January 2026, a 90 percent renewal rate and 90 percent revenue share after the Identity Digital deal, prompting copycat bets such as Slovenia's .si after the US superintelligence executive order. Identifies the concentration of portfolio applicants in contention sets (Link Freedom Group 118, XYZ.COM 100, Registry Services 66, Intercap Registry 54, Radix Technologies 41, ShortDot 32) and closes by splitting the land rush into three layers: rational defensive brand applications, probability-betting portfolio applicants whose risk control was removed by the private-resolution ban, and the structural design where cost is front-loaded, outcomes uncertain and exit windows narrow - noting that transparency does not make it cheap.

### Linux/运维

- [输入邮箱和密码，服务器自己找上来：给自建邮件域做一套 autoconfig](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-10-22_mail-autoconfig-thunderbird-k9-zero-touch-setup/): A hands-on walkthrough of making mail clients configure themselves on a self-hosted domain, so the user only types an email address and password. Starts from the real failure mode: on an Android phone, automatic discovery gave up and the manual setup screen was pre-filled with three wrong values - the hostname had lost its prefix (`.example.com` instead of `mail.example.com`), the port was guessed as 465 when the server used 587, and the username was filled with the full address when the server expected only the local part. Explains the client discovery order that produces these guesses: hardcoded probes for `imap.<domain>` / `mail.<domain>` / `smtp.<domain>`, then RFC 6186 SRV lookups (`_imaps._tcp`, `_submissions._tcp`), then the Mozilla autoconfig XML at `https://autoconfig.<domain>/mail/config-v1.1.xml`, then Mozilla's ISPDB, and finally manual setup. Documents that SRV alone was not enough in practice - K-9 Mail 24.0 still reported no configuration found with only SRV records present, and only started working once the autoconfig XML was served - so SRV is a bonus rather than a sufficient condition. Highlights the single most consequential line in the XML: `%EMAILLOCALPART%` substitutes just the part before the @ while `%EMAILADDRESS%` substitutes the whole address, and most tutorials use the latter, which fails against Dovecot setups that authenticate by system username. Points out the layer most often missed and which fails silently: the TLS certificate must include `autoconfig.<domain>` as a SAN, because clients do standard certificate validation and will not fall back to ignoring the error, illustrated by `curl` reporting a subject name mismatch while `openssl x509 -ext subjectAltName` shows only the mail hostname; the fix is a single `certbot certonly --expand --cert-name <existing> -d <old> -d autoconfig.<domain>` against DNS validation, which needs no downtime and no port 80. Warns that a wildcard record used as an anti-scanning blackhole (`*.example.com A 127.0.0.1`) will shadow the new name so that clients connect to themselves, requiring explicit A/AAAA records since exact matches take precedence over wildcards in DNS. Provides a complete nginx server block that inlines the XML via `location =` plus `return 200` instead of maintaining a separate file, serving it on both 80 and 443, redirecting `/.well-known/autoconfig/mail/config-v1.1.xml`, and adding `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` with `always` so non-2xx responses keep the header. Explains why a Cloudflare Worker was not used: a token scoped to DNS returns No access to the specified resource when writing Worker scripts, and an existing nginx plus Let's Encrypt setup needs no new dependency. Concludes with the central methodological point that no amount of indirect verification (DNS resolves, certificate matches, curl returns the XML) substitutes for the real test - entering only an email address on a device that has never been configured and seeing the configuration-found screen, which in the measured comparison also auto-detected the Sent, Junk and Trash folders that manual setup had missed. Appends a candid postmortem of a self-inflicted outage: probing the submission port with `openssl s_client`, `nc -w`, and `/dev/tcp` produced `errno=111 Connection refused` while the phone was successfully sending mail at the same moment, and the cause was fail2ban's `postfix-scanners` jail whose filter treats `disconnect ... commands=0/0` - connect without speaking SMTP then hang up - as scanner behaviour, which is exactly what those three probes do; the ban action is an iptables REJECT with icmp-port-unreachable, which surface as Connection refused, so the diagnostic tool caused the very symptom it was measuring, and rerunning it fifteen seconds after an unban banned the host again. The durable lessons: Connection refused does not imply a closed port because REJECT produces it too, port probes must speak the real protocol through the 220 banner and EHLO/STARTTLS before concluding reachability, fail2ban `ignoreip` should whitelist the operator's entire IPv6 /64 prefix because privacy addresses rotate within a stable prefix, and the `commands=0/0` rule is aggressive enough to misfire on legitimate clients whose TLS handshake fails. Closes by admitting that the three hypotheses formed during the investigation - the client was using a proxy, the cloud provider blocked submission ports, and the server could not reach itself - were all wrong for the same reason: treating a probe tool's return code as primary evidence while never reading the server log, which had been recording `connect` and `auth=1` the whole time. All domains, IPs and usernames in the article are desensitised placeholders.  - Key topics: autoconfig, autodiscover, Mozilla ISPDB, RFC 6186, SRV record, _imaps._tcp, _submissions._tcp, STARTTLS, implicit TLS, socketType, EMAILLOCALPART, EMAILADDRESS, Dovecot, auth_username_format, Let's Encrypt, certbot --expand, SAN, subjectAltName, wildcard DNS shadowing, nginx location exact match, Access-Control-Allow-Origin, Cloudflare Worker, fail2ban, postfix-scanners, commands=0/0, icmp-port-unreachable, errno 111, ignoreip, IPv6 /64, Thunderbird, K-9 Mail

- [闰秒要在 2027 年 5 月 20 日退役了：而 Linux 已经为此准备了十四年](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-10-19_leap-second-retired-2027-linux-clocks/): Translation+analysis of Tom's Hardware's report and the primary CGPM resolutions, covering the decision by the General Conference on Weights and Measures on 15 October 2026 to move continuous UTC's effective date from 2035 to 20 May 2027 and widen the maximum permitted UT1-UTC difference from one second to 3,600 seconds, retiring the leap second regime that began in 1972. Reproduces the resolution's own three recitals rather than only the news framing: that a March 2025 workshop by the Consultative Committee for Time and Frequency with the IERS estimated the probability of a negative leap second would rise rapidly to 30 percent by 2035; that IoT, dispersed multi-sensor systems, smart grids and virtual services create growing risk of malfunction with any leap second and especially a negative one; and that different global service providers use different mitigation methods to avoid time steps, producing inconsistency between systems and disseminating time and frequency that does not conform to the SI unit, which is the recital most worth singling out because it says the handling of leap seconds has already caused problems rather than that leap seconds are merely dangerous. Notes BIPM's warning that a negative leap second has never been applied and poses high risk of anomalies and disruption to largely unprepared critical infrastructure, with preparation cost estimated as similar to millennium bug preparations, explaining the economic logic as not that leap seconds are bad but that a never-executed negative leap second fails a cost-benefit test given 27 positive ones since 1972 including the 2016 instance where clocks reached 23:59:60 and the 2012 Reddit outage. Then supplies the half Tom's Hardware omits, the Linux side: CLOCK_TAI has existed since kernel 3.10 in 2013 precisely to avoid leap second jumps, with man-pages noting it is derived from wall-clock time but counts leap seconds, does not experience the adjustments CLOCK_REALTIME suffers, has an epoch ten seconds earlier, and degrades to behaving like CLOCK_REALTIME if NTP does not provide the necessary help, plus the man-pages line that appears to predict this decision, that because leap seconds are planned to be discontinued its value will likely remain exactly 37 seconds greater than CLOCK_REALTIME. Quotes Linus Torvalds's 2015 argument for smearing over rare special events because a continuous mechanism is far easier to test and confuses user space less, together with the objection raised then that smearing does not handle CLOCK_TAI properly and that since CLOCK_REALTIME cannot yet be frequency steered separately it ends up slowing CLOCK_TAI and CLOCK_MONOTONIC too, and chrony's documentation which states plainly that this feature must be used carefully because the server intentionally does not serve its best estimate of true time and that clients must only sync with servers smearing identically. Argues the deepest gain is not saving millennium-bug-scale preparation cost but removing a forced choice, since with leap seconds present one must pick between accurate time and continuous time and either choice loses the other, whereas without insertion there is nothing to smear. Covers what changes after May 2027: ordinary users are unlikely to notice if their time servers are updated, CLOCK_REALTIME stops being an approximation that ignores leap seconds and becomes genuinely continuous, the 37-second offset becomes a constant, and software maintaining its own leap second tables should be checked for the case where an event that always happened stops happening. Notes the leap hour alternative is remote, quoting IERS's Christian Bizouard that it postpones the decision and a future generation will decide, and BIPM's defence that many countries already differ from local apparent solar time by more than an hour and that hour changes are regularly introduced with daylight saving time.
  - Key topics: leap second, BIPM, CGPM, 28th CGPM 2026, Resolution 5, continuous UTC, 20 May 2027, UT1-UTC, 3600 seconds, leap hour, negative leap second, 30 percent by 2035, CCTF, IERS, Christian Bizouard, Patrizia Tavella, SI unit, UTC, TAI, CLOCK_TAI, CLOCK_REALTIME, CLOCK_MONOTONIC, 37 seconds, kernel 3.10, man-pages, chrony, leapsecmode, leapsectz, smearing, leap smear, adjtimex, Linus Torvalds, Reddit 2012, 23:59:60, 27 leap seconds, 1972, millennium bug, daylight saving time, 译文


- [为了省下 62 毫秒，Omarchy 用 Claude Code 重写了一个 XDG 脚本：这个数字比它看起来重要](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-10-19_omarchy-browser-launch-xdg-optimization/): Translation+analysis of Phoronix's brief on Omarchy 4.0.5, an Arch Linux distribution built around the Hyprland desktop with 45,141 stars and 5,569 forks as measured on 19 October 2026, created June 2025 and describing itself as beautiful, modern and opinionated Linux. Covers the small change the piece is built on: profiling default browser launching found that calling xdg-settings get default-web-browser cost roughly 72 milliseconds every time because of its tangle of POSIX shell scripts, and David Heinemeier Hansson wrote a replacement helper with Claude Code that does the same work in about ten milliseconds. Explains where the 72 milliseconds goes by walking through what a typical xdg-utils script does (starting a shell interpreter, detecting the desktop environment by reading environment variables and probing while possibly calling D-Bus, loading and merging several mimeapps.list locations, and invoking external tools like sed grep and awk with a fork and exec each), so the cost is one shell start plus many process creations rather than a slow computation. Reproduces the PR description of omarchy-cmd-default-browser as a new hidden helper that reads the x-scheme-handler/http default from the config-dir mimeapps.list files the way xdg-mime does, checking the desktop-specific hyprland-mimeapps.list first and taking the first listed entry that is installed, and highlights two things worth noting: that it reproduces xdg-mime semantics rather than simplifying them, specifically the rule that the first copy of an entry found decides by whether its Exec command still resolves so an entry left behind for a removed browser is skipped even when a system copy of the same entry exists, which prevents the classic why is my default browser setting not taking effect bug; and that it has an explicit fallback chain to xdg-settings, then to xdg-mime for https when BROWSER is unset, exactly as before, so the fast path never changes correctness and worst case reverts to the old behaviour. Notes omarchy-launch-browser and omarchy-launch-webapp now use it, and that another separate optimisation improved the Omarchy shell bar from roughly 20 seconds down to about 15 seconds on a six-monitor setup with many widgets, which contrasts the two shapes of optimisation (a short path taken every time versus a long path taken at session start). Argues the change exposes the cost of portability, since xdg-utils is a pile of shell scripts precisely because it must work on an unknown desktop and check every possibility each call while Omarchy knows it is Hyprland and can write a fast path that only serves itself, and that this trade is sound for an opinionated distribution but not for a general-purpose one serving millions of users. Adds that the 62 milliseconds is barely perceptible in absolute terms since human immediacy thresholds are around 100 milliseconds, so the value is not saving time but eliminating work that should not exist when the core logic needs a single file read. Treats it as a concrete case of rewriting a slow path with AI and argues the five-step method is the reusable part (measure, locate the specific call, understand why it is slow, rewrite while preserving semantics, keep a fallback), with steps four and five being where most rewrites fail because people simplify away the branches that look redundant but actually handle edge cases, and with AI-assisted rewriting carrying a specific risk that a model asked to rewrite tends to produce the mainstream interpretation and drop those branches, which is why identifying which semantics must be preserved is the human judgement that makes the output correct. States the material's limits: the implementation language of the new helper is not given, the hardware behind the 72 and 10 millisecond figures is not stated, and whether the finding was discussed upstream with xdg-utils is unknown, which matters because if xdg-settings is slow on every desktop it is an upstream problem that Omarchy chose to route around locally.
  - Key topics: Omarchy, Arch Linux, Hyprland, Basecamp, David Heinemeier Hansson, DHH, Claude Code, xdg-utils, xdg-settings, xdg-mime, mimeapps.list, hyprland-mimeapps.list, x-scheme-handler/http, desktop entry, Exec command, POSIX shell, fork exec, profiling, 72 milliseconds, 10 milliseconds, 62 milliseconds, omarchy-cmd-default-browser, omarchy-launch-browser, omarchy-launch-webapp, fallback chain, BROWSER variable, portability cost, bar performance, six monitors, Linux 7.2 kernel, BORE scheduler, Qt 6.12, AI-assisted rewrite, semantics preservation, 译文


- [Linux 7.3 是一个「全方位纪录」：两万多个提交、三千多名开发者，而 Phoronix 特意提到了 AI 带来的代码变动](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-10-19_linux-7-3-release-record-commits-ai-churn/): Combined analysis of LWN's and Phoronix's coverage of Linux 7.3, released 18 October 2026, built on the observation that each report contains half of the story. LWN calls it a record-breaker on all fronts with 18,765 non-merge commits from 3,021 developers of whom 807 were first-time kernel developers, while Phoronix describes the final week's bug and regression fixes as including the continued flow of AI/LLM churn. Reproduces Linus Torvalds's release mail in two parts, the joke that he kept his wits together long enough to track the day of the week so the release was not randomly delayed, and the plan that the 7.4 merge window opens the next day while he is on his annual family vacation spending most of the day on a boat and underwater, getting back to merging in the afternoon with an unusual schedule for a while, and notes that kernel release cadence depends on one person's calendar even as 3,021 developers contribute. Lists LWN's feature set (significant binfmt_misc extensions, group-scheduling work aimed at large systems, the new failfs filesystem that fails all operations, the fchroot system call, global per-CPU data for BPF programs, the completion of sched_ext, working-set tracking for virtual machines, alternative data-stream support in ntfs3, and a long list of SMB server improvements) against Phoronix's hardware-oriented list (faster I/O on modern systems, more AMD Zen 6 platform preparations, Steam Controller 2026 driver support, improvements for older AMD GPUs, better vRAM management for systems with limited video memory), noting the two lists barely overlap because one covers subsystem-level capability and the other user-visible hardware and performance. Explains the three features worth singling out: failfs as a deliberate way to make a mount point exist but not fall through to an upper layer, sched_ext's completion marking the end of a long cycle that turns scheduling policy into a replaceable user-programmable component via BPF, and fchroot as a rare new syscall whose interface cannot be changed after release. Then connects the record commit count to AI with care: reports the rc1 figures (15,267 non-merge commits, 2,450 developers, 520 first-time, the second-highest rc1 count in kernel history with only 6.7-rc1 higher because it carried nearly 3,000 commits of bcachefs history), LWN's August prediction that if the 7.2 pattern of over 3,000 post-rc1 commits repeated 7.3 would become the release with the most commits ever, and the outcome of roughly 3,498 post-rc1 commits, while arguing the causal link to AI is not supported by current data for three reasons (the 6.7 record came from a large tree merge, removing all 1,264 Assisted-by commits would still leave 14,003 at rc1, and churn may mean more processing burden rather than more features). Highlights LWN's rc1 statistic that 1,264 commits carried Assisted-by tags just over eight percent while surely a significant undercount of LLM-assisted commits, and explains why that figure must be read as a floor since the tag was being deprecated during the 7.3 cycle after the 8 October Maintainers Summit and Sasha Levin's 9 October removal patch, with Jeff Layton's first reason being that it was not universally followed, so once the tag is gone the participation rate becomes unmeasurable from git history. Adds the two concrete fixes Phoronix mentions (rare, varying SMP boot hangs going back to 2024 and workarounds for Samsung 990 PRO and 990 EVO Plus SSDs lying about capabilities on select firmware) as examples of what churn looks like. Preserves Darrick Wong stepping back after 23 years and his 2023 explanation that XFS contributors were spending most of their time on distro backports and on AI-generated corner-case bug reports that are not user reports, with review becoming a nightmare of sifting through under-documented code, arguing the record commit count and maintainer attrition may be two sides of the same thing and that more commits does not equal faster progress if part of them needs extra human triage. Notes the LTS question remains open between 7.4 (possibly before end of December) and Greg KH declaring 7.3 as this year's LTS.
  - Key topics: Linux 7.3, Linus Torvalds, LWN, Jonathan Corbet, Phoronix, Michael Larabel, 18,765 commits, 3,021 developers, 807 first-time, 15,267 rc1 commits, 2,450 developers, 520 first-time, 6.7-rc1, bcachefs, 3,498 post-rc1, binfmt_misc, group scheduling, failfs, fchroot, BPF per-CPU, sched_ext, working-set tracking, ntfs3, alternative data streams, SMB server, AMD Zen 6, Steam Controller 2026, vRAM management, Assisted-by, 1,264 commits, eight percent, undercount, Maintainers Summit, Sasha Levin, Jeff Layton, AI/LLM churn, SMP boot hangs, Samsung 990 PRO, Samsung 990 EVO Plus, Darrick Wong, XFS, distro backports, AI-generated bug reports, LTS, Greg KH, 译文


- [MIPS 与龙芯的三十年：一家公司放弃了自己的指令集，而一家中国公司在那一年离开了它](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-10-16_mips-loongson-loongarch-history/): Analysis answering two reader questions raised by a SEMI article on MIPS's Physical AI push. Confirms that the MIPS in that article is the same company and instruction set: founded 1984 by Stanford researchers including John L. Hennessy (later Turing Award winner and Stanford president) and Chris Rowen, commercialising the MIPS project (Microprocessor without Interlocked Pipeline Stages), so the company name, ISA name and Stanford project name share one origin. Then establishes the reversal that makes the story interesting: in 2021 the MIPS company announced it was abandoning the MIPS architecture in favour of RISC-V designs, having previewed its first RISC-V cores (eVocore P8700 and I8500) in May 2022, so the year Loongson left MIPS is the same year MIPS left MIPS. Traces how a company that defined an instruction set became a traded asset: SGI's 333 million dollar acquisition in 1992 to secure 64-bit R4000 supply, the 1998 spin-out into an intellectual property licensing company after SGI announced a move to Itanium, complete separation on 20 June 2000, acquisition by Imagination Technologies in 2013, sale to Tallwood Venture Capital in 2017, purchase by Wave Computing in 2018, Wave's bankruptcy in 2020, emergence in 2021 as MIPS with the RISC-V pivot, and acquisition by GlobalFoundries in July 2025, noting the employee count falling from 146 in September 2010 to at most 50 by May 2018 and that the 1998 licensing-company form explains both why Loongson could license MIPS and why the dispute ended up being about the boundaries of that licence. Sets out Loongson's three steps with their precise legal character: licensing from 2007 through a deal between MIPS and the Institute of Computing Technology where STMicroelectronics bought the MIPS licence so the processor could be marketed as MIPS-based or MIPS-compatible rather than MIPS-like, with early implementations omitting four patented MIPS instructions (US4814976A, unaligned load-store) to avoid legal problems; LoongISA 1.0 in 2015 on the Loongson 3A2000 defined as a superset of MIPS64 release 2 with LoongEXT (148 instructions), LoongVZ (5), LoongBT (213, for faster x86 and ARM binary translation at a cost of 5 percent of die area, helping QEMU translate x86 to MIPS with a reported 30 percent penalty), LoongSIMD (1014) and MIPS Release 5 MSA DSP and VZ modules, showing that the early strategy was to add extensions so it could run other people's code efficiently; and LoongArch from 2020, released with the 3A5000 series in 2021, described by Loongson as nearly 2000 instructions and by the kernel documentation as a new RISC ISA somewhat like MIPS and RISC-V with LA32R LA32S and LA64 variants, 32 general registers with r0 fixed at zero, 32 floating-point registers, 128-bit LSX and 256-bit LASX vector extensions that share register space with floating point, four privilege levels and 32-bit fixed-length instructions in nine basic formats. Preserves the kernel documentation's own dividing line that 3A1000 through 3A4000 are MIPS-compatible while 3A5000 and later are based on LoongArch, which puts the boundary between two specific models rather than vaguely in recent years. Covers the arbitration carefully by separating two questions that produced opposite answers: whether Loongson infringed MIPS intellectual property, which six of seven claims being dismissed (including unauthorised modification and use beyond the licence scope) answered no, and whether Loongson owed royalties, which the finding that the 2011 licence transfer to CIP United was valid answered yes, with the 2023 decision adding that Loongson did nothing wrong and caused no damage and should only pay unpaid royalties plus appropriate delay fees while CIP United's own 2025 outlook describes a further 2024 award supporting its licensor status, fee rights including penalties and audit rights. Lays out the dispute's origin from the IPO inquiry reply, including that MIPS transferred the 2011 licence effective 1 April 2019, that Loongson objected from June 2019 but paid 2019 and 2020 Q1 royalties in good faith, that it stopped paying after discovering CIP United's lawsuit against MIPS in California and MIPS entering bankruptcy with Wave, so the dispute began over whether the other party had the standing to collect rather than over a refusal to pay, and lists CIP United's seven claims and its demand that Loongson publicly acknowledge using MIPS technology in present and future publications, which is exactly what the later argument was about. Notes the third-party evidence Loongson relied on (a CESI laboratory report finding the 3A5000 uses LoongArch and not MIPS, and a CCID intellectual property analysis comparing LoongArch against tens of thousands of patents across ALPHA ARM MIPS POWER RISC-V and x86), that the dispute ran during Loongson's IPO with a dedicated risk disclosure and a direct regulator question about whether LoongArch depended on MIPS licensing, and the planned transition from about 70 percent non-MIPS revenue in 2022 to 90 percent in 2023 and no MIPS-based commercial products around 2024. Explains why calling LoongArch a fork of MIPS is not quite right but not quite wrong, since looking like MIPS is largely an engineering consequence of RISC convergence in register count, fixed instruction width and load-store shape while the real differences live in instruction formats, addressing modes, privilege models and vector register organisation, and that patents typically protect mechanisms rather than such common knowledge, so similarity as an engineering outcome and independence as a legal finding can both hold. Highlights as the most substantive disclosure of the piece Loongson's own account that building an ecosystem around a new ISA depends on a 3+3 base: three compilers (GCC, LLVM, GoLang) and three virtual machines (Java, JavaScript, .NET), plus its observation that MIPS's weak market share left few people maintaining its software ecosystem so Loongson itself had long been its maintainer, which explains how LoongArch got usable toolchains quickly. Closes by noting MIPS's current IP lineup is essentially RISC-V with the name as its remaining MIPS legacy, that Loongson reportedly won a case about rights to use MIPS in January 2024 and shipped LoongArch-based 3C6000 server chips in June 2025 with a claim of no foreign technology licensing or overseas supply chain, and that the two principals left MIPS in the same year for different reasons while the instruction set itself is still in use under different ownership.
  - Key topics: MIPS, MIPS Technologies, MIPS Computer Systems, Stanford, John L. Hennessy, Chris Rowen, RISC, MIPS64, MIPS32, Loongson, 龙芯, LoongArch, LoongISA, LA32R, LA32S, LA64, LSX, LASX, LoongEXT, LoongVZ, LoongBT, LoongSIMD, LoongMMI, SGI, Silicon Graphics, R4000, Itanium, Imagination Technologies, PowerVR, Tallwood Venture Capital, Wave Computing, GlobalFoundries, CIP United, 芯联芯, HKIAC arbitration, PA21030, US4814976A, unaligned load-store, binary translation, QEMU, CESI laboratory, CCID, IPO inquiry reply, 3A1000, 3A2000, 3A4000, 3A5000, 3C6000, GCC, LLVM, GoLang, Java, JavaScript, .NET, RISC-V, RVA23, Physical AI, ARC, 自主可控


- [Windows 桌面测试为什么难自动化：因为一个容器里没有登录会话，而人得先登进去](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-10-16_windows-desktop-automation-disposable-vms/): Translation+analysis of QA Wolf's writeup on running Windows desktop app tests at enterprise scale, flagged as a vendor blog whose product is named in the title and which supplies no performance, cost or concurrency figures. Leads with the core insight that they stopped treating Windows machines as servers and treated them like phones instead, a device a test claims, uses once and throws away, and the root constraint that makes it necessary: Windows UI Automation only works inside an active logged-in desktop session, so a machine that is merely switched on is not enough, which cannot be engineered away because it follows from UIA's original purpose as the accessibility interface served to a person actually using the computer. Organises the six constraints as a dependency chain rather than a list (a full VM is needed because Windows containers have no graphical desktop, so cold start costs two to three minutes, and someone must log in, and machines remember installed files registry keys profiles and stray processes, and every app brings its own installers admin prompts licensed dependencies and first-run dialogs, and there is no built-in visibility unless you build it), plus the environment note that tooling assumes Linux because Kubernetes and CI runners were designed around Linux containers. Explains the architecture borrowed from their mobile infrastructure with two extensions to the device model (a device need not live inside the cluster, and a claim can return desktop connection addresses including CDP), the three parts of controller, Linux runner pod and Windows VM, and the three connections of CDP for browsers, Appium with WinAppDriver over UIA for native apps, and a WebRTC screen stream for live viewing and recording. Covers the three key designs and why each follows: single-use VMs eliminating a whole category of passes-alone-fails-in-suite problems, warm pools absorbing boot time with a reconciler that advances each VM one step per short pass and writes progress onto its record so a slow boot never blocks anything else, and updates by attrition meaning a new machine image needs no upgrade process at all, with the image produced by a PowerShell script published to a GCE image family so nobody hand-maintains a golden machine. Details what the image must pre-bake (Appium and WinAppDriver installed configured and running inside a live desktop session before the first test arrives, a separate root-level session for notifications and the Action Center, common software like Chrome and Acrobat, and variants such as an Office image that clears Word's first-run dialogs before a test ever sees them). Explains why test code stays on Linux and controls the VM remotely, the single API that hides which protocol carries each step while keeping the distinction between browser and native app visible, and the signed-URL design where app files never pass through the runner and only a central API service can sign short-lived URLs while unprivileged test code requests downloads through a trusted parent process. Closes by noting the transferable judgements, including that when both sides of a tradeoff are bad the right move is to question the tradeoff itself (replacing cleanup with lifecycle), that abandoning in-place upgrades can make upgrades unmanaged by turning an operations action into a build action, that the borrowed-interface boundary explains why the phone analogy holds where it does, and that the cost structure of cloud VMs is what makes disposability easier than on physical devices, while stating the material's gaps on performance, cost and scale.

- [两个「隐含假设」的修正：CPU boost 该不该默认开，复用缓冲区能不能只拷最新那帧](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-10-16_cppc-boost-default-mutter-damage-tracking/): Translation+analysis of two unrelated Phoronix items that both fix an implicitly accepted assumption. On the kernel side, a Huawei patch proposes enabling CPU boost by default in the generic ACPI CPPC CPUFreq driver used on many ARM64 Linux server platforms, where boost has been off by default for processors whose highest performance level exceeds nominal and required setting the boost option via sysfs; the stated reason is that this is a poor default for server platforms where peak performance is usually wanted, and that it avoids requiring userspace to set it manually. Preserves Arm engineer Christian Loehle's reply in full, which questions the mechanism rather than the default: that the power and thermal envelope on modern silicon is complex enough that boost has little meaning, that it in no way guarantees no throttling or that you receive the requested performance, that a silicon-aware user can always set individual ceilings via scaling_max_freq so it works for their platform, workload and environment combination, and his curiosity about the usage behind a Huawei-introduced commit given that having a platform with NOMINAL_PERF != HIGHEST_PERF is just additional headache on Linux for now. Argues this reply contains two arguments of different weight, that boost does not do what its name suggests, and that a boolean switch may be an unnecessary layer of indirection over directly setting a frequency ceiling, and connects it to the same week's AMD Zen 6 client CPPC changes where hard-coded values were added because those platforms need a maximum frequency per core type for capacity calculations until a future ACPI revision provides a proper interface. On the desktop side, covers Ray Strode's Mutter change adding damage tracking for secondary GPU copy buffers, first appearing in GNOME 51.2 rather than GNOME 52, with his three-part diagnosis reproduced as a table: the primary-GPU copy rotates through three destination buffers so a reused buffer can be several frames old and copying only the newest damage leaves older pixels behind; the serialized secondary-GPU copy has a valid two-frame assumption only while every copy succeeds, and failures can make its damage history disagree with the buffer contents; and the CPU fallback copies the whole frame but currently returns a buffer after a failed read, while a successful zero-copy interval can leave fallback buffers older than their recorded state. Covers the fix, MetaSecondaryGpuCopyState, which records the last successful source frame in each destination buffer and keeps damage from recent frames, with three boundary rules worth noting: unknown or too-old buffers receive the whole frame, as do regions with more than 16 rectangles, buffer selection advances only after a successful copy, and a successful zero-copy import invalidates the fallback state. Argues the pair diverge in how they treat a questionable assumption, one changing a default while the other makes the assumption explicit as state with conservative fallbacks, and that the second approach demonstrates the standard an optimisation must meet to keep existing. Closes by preserving Phoronix's note that Strode's code was written a month earlier but initially held up over concerns that some commit messages were AI/LLM-generated slop, connecting it to LLVM's RFC reason that AI-written PR descriptions deprive contributors of the chance to understand and express what a PR does as a sanity check.
  - Key topics: ACPI, CPPC, Collaborative Processor Performance Control, CPU boost, sysfs, scaling_max_freq, NOMINAL_PERF, HIGHEST_PERF, ARM64 servers, AMD Zen 6, hard-coded frequencies, Mutex, GNOME, Mutter, compositor, damage tracking, secondary GPU copy buffers, MetaSecondaryGpuCopyState, multi-GPU, hybrid laptops, GPU buffers, CPU fallback, zero-copy, Ray Strode, Christian Loehle, castkms, Pronk, Google Cast, AI-generated commit messages, LLM slop, 译文


- [Ubuntu 26.10 用 Sequoia 换掉 GnuPG 签名：发行版第一次把「量子威胁」写进了自己的包管理器](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-10-16_ubuntu-26-10-stonking-stingray/): Translation+analysis of Canonical's official announcement of Ubuntu 26.10, codenamed Stonking Stingray, released 15 October 2026, organised by who is affected rather than by component, and explicitly noting that two items in this release were already covered separately on this site (the completed Rust coreutils migration and the Myna speech-to-text preview). Separates the package signing change into two different things that Canonical's single sentence conflates: replacing GnuPG with Sequoia PGP to verify APT repository signatures, which pays off immediately by removing a class of memory-safety bugs from the component that decides what code may be installed as root, versus post-quantum readiness, which is a schedule problem because signatures made today have to remain trustworthy for years across release media and long-lived archives, analogous to harvest-now-decrypt-later but for signing; and notes that quantum-safe token support through openCryptoki with PKCS #11 V3.2 coverage across Soft, EP11 and CCA tokens plus ML-DSA and ML-KEM matters because enterprise key material often cannot leave hardware, so algorithm support without hardware support cannot land in regulated environments. Explains the dbus-broker change in detail: per-app message accounting replaces legacy queuing so a single misbehaving application cannot stall the whole desktop, contrasting the previous first-come-first-served scheduling that lets one runaway app create a system-wide stall whose cause is hard to locate, and arguing this class of improvement is hard to promote because it shows up as something no longer breaking rather than as a new feature. Explains TPM-backed full-disk encryption extending to models lacking a hardware root of trust, where requiring a PIN or passphrase supplies a different factor when the machine itself cannot provide a verifiable starting point, and argues this is better than either dropping support or enabling silently without stating the strength difference. Covers kernel 7.3 enabling Intel Xe3P Nova Lake, AMD Zen 6 and NVIDIA 615 with the DRM and power management hooks heterogeneous platforms need, plus out-of-the-box Lustre support, GNOME 51, Ubuntu App Center consistency for snaps and debs, improved Orca support for Flutter applications, adjusted desktop OOM scoring, Microsoft identity integration covering password with MFA and passwordless authentication so Linux machines sit under the same security umbrella as Windows ones, a dedicated amd64v3 installer, RISC-V desktop images including first support for RVA23-enabled SpacemiT K3 silicon with the quoted comment from RISC-V International's CEO, ROCm 10.0 with vLLM and SGLang support, and upstream toolchains LLVM 22.1.6, GCC 15.2.0, Python 3.14.7, Rust 1.97.1, Zig 0.16 and Go 1.27 plus Spring AI and Rust devpacks. Argues the most representative single item is swapping GnuPG for Sequoia because it shows both characteristics of the release, rewriting critical components in modern languages and preparing for long-horizon security problems, and that the value of both lies in the future rather than today.

- [systemd v262 那 35 条改动，真正的主线是把「启动信任」变成一条可以逐段签名的链](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-10-16_systemd-v262-trust-chain-varlink/): Analysis of systemd v262, released 22 September 2026, based on the official NEWS file rather than the Mastodon post index the reader supplied (which lists 35 posts by Lennart Poettering but is not itself a changelog). Identifies two threads running through those changes rather than reciting them. The first is finer-grained boot trust: NvPCRs now use a write policy permitting only the initial extend from the initrd environment and no longer rely on an anchor secret sealed to the TPM, with all NvPCR definitions required in the UKI plus a signed PCR policy bound to the initrd boot phase created via ukify's --sign-initrd-pcrs; new --policyref options on systemd-measure and matching --tpm2-public-key-policyref on cryptenroll and repart allow an initrd-only signed policy without reusing the same signature in later boot phases; read-only ESP support in systemd-boot and systemd-stub; verification of a generated EK against its certificate before persisting it with preference for high-range templates; and Encrypt= combined with Verity=data where repart writes LUKS2 ciphertext first then builds dm-verity metadata over that ciphertext so verity is the outer authenticity envelope and LUKS2 the inner encryption layer, described as authenticated confidentiality, with the argument that the ordering is not arbitrary because authenticity must be verifiable and confidentiality must be the layer that sees plaintext. The second thread is Varlink steadily replacing D-Bus, with the announcement that the experimental systemd-sysupdated D-Bus API will be removed in v263 in favour of clients talking directly to systemd-sysupdate over Varlink, plus new Varlink interfaces for cryptenroll enrolment, sysinstall, journal following and systemd-report signing, the last taking signatures from backend Varlink signers linked into /run/systemd/report.sign, and experimental --introspect-cli exposing machine-readable command metadata as JSON so scripts need not parse --help, explicitly flagged as unstable. Also covers ActivatingConcurrencyMax on slice units, atomic job enqueueing via EnqueueUnitJobMany and atomic tag add/remove, key=value machine tags, first-boot recovery key enrolment via systemd-cryptenroll-firstboot.service, rogue TPM protection for LUKS enrolments, fscrypt v2 in homed with no in-place v1 to v2 policy upgrade, the ordering discipline in LUKS-backed home password rotation that adds replacement keyslots before removing old ones so an enrolment failure does not lock the user out, SHA384 and SHA512 PCR bank consideration, execution from dm-verity protected filesystems while still denying the writable upper layer, static single-binary service manager builds, dm-clone boot integration via /etc/clonetab with region-size control, FONT_SCALE for vconsole with out-of-range values clamped, word-list-based hostname wildcards where ? resolves to a hashed hex character and $ picks a word from a list, kernel coredump socket protocol support from Linux 6.17 with systemd-coredumpd listening on /run/systemd/coredumpd/kernel and the caveat that changing coredump.conf requires reloading that service, Intel TDX CoCo support in vmspawn with system credentials for CoCo VMs, KExecCount and prior kexec shutdown timestamps surfaced through systemd-analyze time, the DNS-SD registration fix explaining that client tracking never worked due to a bug so clients must now keep the bus connection open while one-shot registrations are withdrawn on tool exit, the removal of deprecated Meson options, the tightening that Type=notify-reload services must catch or block ReloadSignal when sending READY=1 or fail to start with a protocol error, and tmpfiles rejecting non-empty argument fields for line types that do not use them. Argues the version's real theme is making the granularity of trust match the granularity of what is being trusted, praises the verity-inside-LUKS2 ordering as a general lesson about stacking security properties, explains why the Varlink direction is about removing a relay when the relay only forwards one process's capability, and closes by noting that the two forward-looking removal notices each state why removal is safe plus a version number, and that the strictness changes show a preference for failing early and clearly over silent tolerance.

- [红帽的两篇新文章，讲的其实是同一件事：当 AI 让「发现漏洞」变便宜之后](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-10-15_red-hat-lightwell-backport-netops-as-code/): Analysis of two Red Hat blog posts from 14 October 2026, explicitly treated as vendor marketing rather than neutral reporting (both authored by product marketing managers and ending in product calls to action), with the third-party figures attributed as Red Hat's citation rather than verified. Leads with the contradiction the figures expose: 95 percent of component downloads already have a fix available (Sonatype 2026 State of the Software Supply Chain Report) while mean time to remediation for complex enterprise applications is 5 months and 10 days (Qualys Enterprise Patch & Remediation Benchmark 2026), and 45 percent of discovered vulnerabilities in large enterprises remain unpatched after 12 months with more than 17 percent rated high or critical (Edgescan 2025 Vulnerability Statistics Report), so the bottleneck is no longer discovery but the cost of changing production. Explains why upgrading is hard by preserving Red Hat's causal chain: applications are built tested and certified against specific library versions, upgrades can introduce breaking changes in production, upgrading one library often requires configuration changes across dependent services with end-to-end verification, regulated industries face expensive recertification or rigid change control, and when a full application rebuild is required the process stretches from days to months, which is why teams create private forks that then require the patch to be reapplied for every subsequent change. Covers Lightwell, the joint Red Hat and IBM initiative providing signed backported security fixes for eligible third-party open source dependencies so applications can be patched at pinned production versions, with its four capabilities (enterprise remediation by Red Hat and IBM engineers validating vulnerabilities and delivering signed backported fixes, clearinghouse intelligence from anonymised cross-institution context, upstream contribution after applicable embargo windows to avoid long-term private fork burden, and compliance artifacts including SBOMs and CSAF/VEX), and adds the three boundaries the article omits: eligibility means a bounded set, backporting is human-engineering-intensive which determines cost and scalability, and it removes the breaking-change risk but not the change cost. Highlights the single most useful sentence on AI governance, that AI is assisting with risk-based routing decisions for patches while approval steps have been added to ensure human oversight, breaking the workflow into AI for ordering and routing, humans for approval and automation for execution, and argues this holds because ordering is verifiable after the fact while approval carries responsibility, matching the same conclusion as the four open source AI policies where the kernel states that only humans can legally certify the DCO, and generalises it to asking who can tell when a judgement is wrong. Lists the eight automation functions including rollback on failure and audit report generation as first-class rather than exception handling. Then covers the NetOps-as-Code post: the automation orchestrator generally available as an add-on for Ansible Automation Platform 2.7 described as a composable workflow canvas; eleven collection releases this quarter (ansible.netcommon 8.6.0 8.6.1 8.6.2, cisco.ios 11.5.0 11.5.1, cisco.iosxr 12.4.0 12.4.1 12.4.2, cisco.nxos 12.1.0, arista.eos 12.2.0, ansible.utils 6.1.0) across three themes of more security-focused (removing outdated pycrypto from unit test requirements, remediating deprecated ansible.module_utils imports, restructuring CI so secret-free jobs run against untrusted pull requests while privileged jobs stay label-gated, vendoring libssh 0.12.2 in ansible-pylibssh wheels, and handling the enable prompt correctly under TACACS+ in arista.eos), more predictable (fixes concentrated in resource module state handling because an incorrect diff means an incorrect change on the device, with specific BGP route-map prefix-list ASDOT VPLS and idempotency fixes in cisco.ios, trunk VLAN and switchport fixes in cisco.nxos, and ACE context fixes in arista.eos, plus crash fixes in fact gathering), and easier to manage (huge_tree support for NETCONF, network_cli transcript recording for troubleshooting and audit, cli_config pushing configuration and detecting changes on platforms lacking native diff, and resolving an intermittent datastore-locked error); notes the testing approach where cisco.ios runs CISSHGO-based Molecule scenarios across all 32 resource modules exercising both libssh and paramiko paths without physical hardware, and the discipline of bounding retries in the cv_deploy role rather than retrying indefinitely. Covers the partner ecosystem entries for Arista AVD (open source Python framework packaged as a certified collection, abstracting network configuration into data models that generate EOS configurations documentation and ANTA validation tests, with IPv6 expansion schema explorer multiprocessing and workspace synchronisation) and NetBox Labs (88 modules plus dynamic inventory and lookup plugins, with Event-Driven Ansible firing job templates by webhook). Closes by arguing the two posts document the same shift, that the AI boundary in the workflow is the most transferable design, that the NetOps details evidence maturity through fixes that only appear in real environments plus a test-coverage description expressed as modules times connection paths without hardware, and by giving three questions to ask when evaluating such offerings: the size of the eligible dependency set, whether the reader's remediation time is dominated by compatibility risk or approval queues, and whether backported fixes return upstream.

- [RISC-V 最尴尬的一个问题终于要解决了：怎么知道「我这台机器符不符合 RVA23」](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-10-15_riscv-rva23-hwprobe-detection/): Translation+analysis of Phoronix's report and Guodong Xu's LPC 2026 presentation, explaining that until October 2026 answering whether a RISC-V system is RVA23 compliant required checking hwprobe or prctl queries for every mandatory extension because the kernel had no one-shot way to report it. Explains what RVA23 is from the specification's own framing that it aligns 64-bit application processor implementations so binary software ecosystems can rely on a large set of guaranteed extensions and a small number of discoverable coarse-grain options, and preserves the explicit non-goal that allowing more hardware implementation flexibility through a minimal feature set plus many fine-grain extensions was deliberately rejected, so RVA23 tightens rather than loosens, which is what makes a general binary possible; explains why the gap matters practically since distributions such as Ubuntu 25.10 and later target RVA23 while compliant hardware remains limited, so a missing extension surfaces as SIGILL rather than a comprehensible error. Reproduces the presentation's comparison of who knows the baseline across architectures: x86-64 with named levels v2 v3 v4, distributions building for v1 with RHEL 10 at v3, and glibc computing the level; arm64 with Armv8.x-a and Armv9.x-a levels, all distributions at Armv8.0-A, and nobody computing it so applications see only feature bits; RISC-V with RVA20 and RVA23, distributions moving from RV64GC to RVA23 on Ubuntu 25.10 and later, and glibc libgcc and each application each computing their own. Uses that to explain the two-answers problem where GCC 16.1's libgcc checks 24 of the 39 mandatory extensions with 6 unchecked and 9 invisible while Canonical's checker performs 40 checks with 3 hwprobe keys needing kernel 7.3 for five of them, and where Zic64b has no bit at all. Details the patch design: riscv_hwprobe(KEY_BASE_BEHAVIOR) returning a bitmask of IMA (rv64ima, user ISA 2.2, priv 1.10) and RVA23U64 (all mandatory extensions), computed once at boot from the full ISA bitmap, with RFC v1 by Andrew Jones in February 2026 carried on by Guodong Xu to v8 in September; highlights three design decisions (turning 39 checks into one bit, computing once at boot so the answer is consistent and costs nothing per call, and the long refinement process), and lists the presentation's four questions directed at the right decision-makers (kernel maintainers on whether the shape is right, distributions on shipping rva23u64 builds of selected libraries, kernel maintainers on deprecating the V prctl, and the room on one enable model for future extensions). Covers the unresolved V extension problem where prctl can revoke it so AT_HWCAP still reports it while hwprobe does not, producing SIGILL before main, and places it in the presentation's three-enable-model comparison across x86-64 (AVX-512 always-on, AMX dynamically enabled per process, CET opt-in), arm64 (SVE and SME always-on with first-use trap allocating state, BTI GCS MTE opt-in) and RISC-V (V always-on but revocable with first-use trap, Zicfilp and Zicfiss opt-in), including the x86 AMX state machine of requesting permission via arch_prctl then trapping on first tile use then checking the signal stack and either resuming or raising SIGILL. Covers how distributions would use the bit with glibc-hwcaps, mirroring x86 where ld.so opens glibc-hwcaps/x86-64-v3/libc.so.6 based on a level glibc computes from CPUID, while on RISC-V ld.so would read the kernel's RVA23U64 bit and open glibc-hwcaps/rva23u64/libc.so.6, with per-function dispatch by CPU model inside; argues this is the core shift because the level moves from being computed by each downstream to being provided by the kernel. Notes the status that most of the series is queued in RISC-V's for-next for Linux 7.4 but the RVA23U64 bit reporting patches are being reworked for at least one more review round, and closes by arguing the real substance is centralising the definition of the baseline in the kernel, that the two-sources-of-truth problem with the V extension is the more worrying issue because it fails before main, that interface review takes long on purpose because a published interface is hard to change, that the bit gives hardware vendors a reproducible way to verify their own compliance claims, and that encoding an external specification's membership list into the kernel is a durable maintenance cost worth paying over inconsistent downstream answers.
  - Key topics: RISC-V, RVA23, RVA23U64, RVA20, profile, 39 mandatory extensions, Zic64b, V vector extension, hwprobe, prctl, AT_HWCAP, SIGILL, KEY_BASE_BEHAVIOR, IMA, RISCV_HWPROBE_BASE_BEHAVIOR, Guodong Xu, Andrew Jones, Qualcomm, Linux 7.4, for-next, LPC 2026 Prague, glibc-hwcaps, libgcc, GCC 16.1, Canonical checker, xypron, Heinrich Schuchardt, Ubuntu 25.10, RV64GC, CPUID, x86-64-v3, AMX, arch_prctl, AVX-512, SVE, SME, MTE, Zicfilp, Zicfiss, signal frame, enable model, Documentation contract, 译文


- [Cloud Hypervisor 54 承诺「前两个版本可迁移」：把一条口头保证变成了可执行的承诺](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-10-15_cloud-hypervisor-54-live-migration/): Translation+analysis of Phoronix's report and the v54.0 release notes published 14 October 2026, for a Rust-based virtual machine monitor that began as an Intel open source project and became a multi-vendor Linux Foundation project. Leads with the most consequential change being a compatibility guarantee rather than a feature: from this release Cloud Hypervisor accepts live migrations from the two previous releases (n-2), so v54.0 accepts migrations from v52.0 and v53.0, upgrades spanning more releases might work but incremental upgrades such as v54 to v56 to v58 are strongly recommended, new functionality is added in a way that keeps VMs from older releases working so only newly created VMs can use it, and the migration protocol version is now an internal detail; explains why this reframes an operational question that previously required knowing protocol versions into one answerable from version numbers alone, notes the honest boundary that migrating back to an older release is not officially supported and may work depending on configuration but with no guarantee, and argues the third rule about new features only applying to new VMs is what keeps the window workable. Covers VFIO device live migration for migratable devices such as ConnectX VFs bound to mlx5_vfio_pci, where device state travels with the guest and memory written by the device is tracked during migration, requiring iommufd and a host driver with migration support and passing pre-opened descriptors on the destination through the new vfio_fds and iommufd_fd options, with the limitation that VFIO devices behind a virtual IOMMU cannot be migrated yet. Covers live migration cancellation via the new vm.cancel-migration API endpoint and ch-remote cancel-migration command, allowing management software to abort a migration that does not converge, whose destination is no longer the best choice, or that puts too much load on the network, with the VM continuing on the source and a vm.migration-cancelled event emitted, and Cloud Hypervisor attempting to restore the source VM to its pre-migration state after a failed or cancelled migration. Covers the event monitor now being properly documented with its format and all events, aiming to keep events stable so management software can rely on them, the new vmm.started event signalling the VMM is ready to serve API requests, and refined migration events. Highlights the VM Generation ID device fix as the highest-consequence change by far: previously all VMs restored from the same snapshot started with the same random number generator state and produced identical /dev/urandom output until reseeded, so a generation ID whose value changes on every restore and incoming live migration is now always present with no configuration, and guest kernels built with CONFIG_VMGENID reseed after restore, with the boundary that applications that seeded their own RNG keep that state and must draw fresh randomness themselves; explains that cloning from one snapshot makes multiple VMs emit identical random bytes, undermining TLS session keys SSH keys tokens and salts, that the failure mode is random state restored too uniformly rather than insufficient randomness, and generalises to asking which state breaks when copied. Also covers experimental ARM SMMUv3 emulation on AArch64 using iommufd to offload translation to the physical SMMUv3 with the guest using its stock arm-smmu-v3 driver, enabling assignment of devices that use the IOMMU themselves such as NVIDIA Grace-Blackwell GPUs, with limits (needs KVM and iommufd and nested translation support, no hotplug snapshot restore or live migration, cannot mix with virtio-iommu); balloon statistics via vm.balloon-stats API and ch-remote and D-Bus; flat VMDK support gated behind backing_files=on with relative extent paths confined to the descriptor's directory and synchronous I/O only and Landlock rules required; faster memory prefault reducing a 3 TiB guest's prefault on a two-socket host from 51.8 seconds to 7.4 seconds by prefaulting per NUMA node in parallel, now backed by transparent huge pages under madvise; AArch64 boot improvements including firmware-aided direct kernel boot via fw_cfg and ACPI-based direct boot enabling PCI hotplug without firmware plus a new ACPI Time and Alarm Device and SMBIOS tables; snapshot and restore improvements including 5 to 9 times faster vCPU state save and restore, about 29 percent smaller serialised state for a 16-disk VM, copy-on-write memory restore mode, and preserve_source; SEV-SNP memory roughly halved with VFIO devices and hotplug huge pages and virtual IOMMU now rejected; the AMD HyperTransport range reserved so VFIO DMA mappings no longer fail above 1011 GiB; and PCI host bridges only on segment 0 so NVIDIA Grace GPUs can be assigned device 0. Closes by arguing the compatibility design is the most transferable lesson (choose the window width, fix when state is snapshotted, hide version negotiation), that the VM Generation ID fix shows a virtualisation-specific risk class where snapshot copies state that should not be copied, and that the correct way to assess such a release is to read the correctness fixes rather than the feature list since they are the ones that bite at scale.
