- [NPU 终于能用 PyTorch 跑了：Mesa 接下这件事，靠的是一条被 AI 加速行业忽略的捷径](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-10-14_mesa-torx-yolox-pytorch-npu/): Translation+analysis of Phoronix's brief, Mesa's own Torx documentation and the developer's blog posts, covering the merge of YOLOX support into Mesa's Torx code in October 2026 for Mesa 26.3. Explains that Torx is Mesa's ExecuTorch backend, implemented as a custom backend for the ExecuTorch on-device AI framework so that portions of a model graph run on NPUs or GPUs, and that it sits beside Teflon (the existing TensorFlow Lite delegate) with both sharing the same Gallium ML API, giving a three-layer structure of framework adapters, a shared Gallium ML API, and hardware drivers (ethosu for Arm Ethos-U, etnaviv for Vivante used in NXP i.MX 8M Plus and Amlogic A311D, rocket for reverse-engineered Rockchip NPUs supported from mainline kernel 6.18, and thames for TI C7x DSPs as found on BeagleY-AI boards). Reports the measured result: YOLOX-Nano at 416x416 quantized to 8-bit integers on an i.MX93 board with an Arm Ethos-U65 running at 17 milliseconds per frame, around 59 frames per second, with the convolutions running entirely on the U65 and the final decoding steps on the CPU because they need floating point. Argues the interesting part is that graphics and AI accelerator drivers have the same engineering shape, so user-mode driver translation of a graph into hardware commands, intermediate representation and optimisation (NIR), memory and buffer management (GEM), and task submission and scheduling (DRM scheduler) are all isomorphic, which is why reuse is not opportunistic but a consequence of abstractions that happen to line up, and notes Tomeu Vizoso's XDC2025 plan to use NIR for optimisation passes and lowering models to hardware. Traces the timeline from Teflon merging into Mesa 24.1 in January 2024 as a TensorFlow Lite delegate originally for Etnaviv, the Arm Ethos Gallium3D driver merging in October 2025 for Mesa 25.3, Thames for TI C7x DSPs in January 2026, Ethos U85 support in March 2026 for Mesa 26.1 (advertised as 20 percent more energy efficient than U55/U65 and scaling from 128 to 2048 MAC units), the mainline Ethos-U driver merging into Linux 6.19 in July 2026 written by Rob Herring, YOLOX running on the Etnaviv driver in August 2026 in partnership with Ideas On Board, and this Torx merge in October 2026. Covers the kernel-side design decisions: driving Ethos-U directly from the main CPU to bypass the Cortex-M companion core and therefore the firmware, because SoC vendors said Cortex-M mediation prevented ML models from co-executing efficiently on CPU and NPU and made deploying new models cumbersome, plus another complaint that Arm's open-source Ethos-U stack was not pre-integrated into the distributions vendors use and lacked a standard path for contributing changes back, with the driver using established DRM practices for UAPI and reusing GEM and the GPU DRM scheduler, merged for Linux 6.19 supporting i.MX93 from the start. Highlights the AOT point as the most important technical idea: unlike TensorFlow Lite, ExecuTorch compiles models in a step separate from execution, so a model can be compiled on a different machine from the target where more expensive optimisations than edge-class hardware could run are practical, which breaks the self-reinforcing loop where weaker devices get less optimisation budget. Describes the test infrastructure (which validates individual operators against CPU references, fetching models from a separate npu-model-zoo repository and running test_torx directly on the NPU board comparing each .pte against the CPU reference) and singles out split_torx_tests.py --ranges, which splits a model into cumulative prefix subgraphs rather than individual ops so a whole-model accuracy failure can be binary-searched to the offending operator while reproducing the real partitioning decisions for every prefix. Records honestly the current limits: Torx works today with the ethosu driver only, the Etnaviv driver should have all operations supported but still lacks the infrastructure work for use with Torx, performance is currently very low because there are no optimisations yet, the final YOLOX decoding runs on the CPU, and other NPU drivers will only be usable from ExecuTorch once they support the ahead-of-time compilation extension to the Gallium ML API. Notes build requirements (meson with -Dtorx=true and at least one NPU-capable Gallium driver, a nightly ExecuTorch wheel because only the nightly ships the executorch.pc pkg-config file Torx needs) and the micro-NPU performance observation that Ethos-U parts with far fewer compute units can match NPUs with up to six times more, attributed to a clean architecture and an excellent software stack yielding good occupancy rates, which reinforces that throughput depends more on keeping the hardware fed than on peak arithmetic. Closes by arguing the news is really about Mesa becoming an accelerator runtime rather than merely a GPU library, that this makes supporting a new NPU a matter of writing one backend against an existing shared layer rather than waiting for a vendor SDK, that the AOT insight generalises to asking whether preparatory work must happen in the weak execution environment at all, and that the limits mean PyTorch support arrives one driver at a time.
  - Key topics: Mesa, Torx, ExecuTorch, Teflon, Gallium ML API, NIR, GEM, DRM scheduler, DRM/accel subsystem, NPU, YOLOX, YOLOX-Nano, PyTorch, TensorFlow Lite, i.MX93, Arm Ethos-U65, Ethos U85, ethosu driver, Etnaviv, Vivante VIP, Rockchip Rocket, Thames, TI C7x DSP, BeagleY-AI, Tomeu Vizoso, Rob Herring, Ideas On Board, Cortex-M bypass, Vela, ahead-of-time compilation, operator fusion, quantisation, 8-bit integers, occupancy, npu-model-zoo, split_torx_tests, Linux 6.19, Mesa 26.3, 译文

- [Asterinas 0.19：用 Rust 重构内核的另一种思路，是「不减少地址空间，只减少 unsafe」](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-10-13_asterinas-0-19-framekernel/): Translation+analysis of LWN's brief and the official Asterinas 0.19.0 announcement, covering a Rust operating system kernel and its framekernel architecture, with repository metrics measured via the GitHub API on 13 October 2026 (asterinas/asterinas, created 17 May 2022, 4,946 stars, 390 forks, 341 open issues, Rust, MPL-2.0). Explains the architecture by framing the long-standing trade-off between monolithic kernels (single address space, fast intra-component calls, no isolation) and microkernels (separate address spaces, IPC cost, per-component isolation), then showing that framekernel changes the axis rather than the address space: the entire OS stays in one address space like a monolithic kernel but is partitioned into a privileged Framework akin to a microkernel which alone may use unsafe Rust, and unprivileged Services which must be safe Rust, so the memory safety of the whole kernel reduces to that of a minimal framework, officially summarised as the speed of a monolithic kernel with the security of a microkernel. States the boundary conditions of that argument honestly (it rests on safe Rust actually being safe and on unsafe genuinely being contained, and it does not address logic bugs), and highlights the measurable unsafe budget as the release's most valuable number: all code needing unsafe lives in OSTD's virtualisation module, about 2,000 lines today, so everything above it up to a complete hypervisor can be safe Rust. Covers the project scale (over 100 contributors ever, more than 250,000 lines with about 200,000 of them Rust, 55 contributors in this release of whom 31 were first-time) and the two-to-three-month release cadence. Then walks the seven headline changes: graphics with a new DRM subsystem providing the DRM core, /dev/dri device nodes, GEM dumb buffers and KMS objects, letting Asterinas NixOS run Xorg on the standard modesetting driver with Mesa software OpenGL instead of fbdev, demonstrated with two 3D games; AArch64 as a fourth architecture after x86-64, RISC-V and LoongArch, described as minimal but usable, bringing up GICv3, the generic timer, PL031 RTC, PL011 UART and virtio-mmio on QEMU's virt machine and running a BusyBox shell with vDSO, entering as a Tier 2 platform with CI coverage still growing, plus Arm machines working as development hosts through linux/arm64 Docker images and an aarch64-linux Nix shell; secure containers as a guest kernel for Kata Containers and Confidential Containers, where the argument is that a memory-safe guest kernel removes a whole class of exploitable bugs from the sandbox, backed by a rewritten overlayfs that doubles the cases it passes in xfstests, mount propagation and the fd-based fsopen syscall family that container runtimes and newer systemd use, a matured virtio-fs driver gaining mmap, O_DIRECT, rename, symbolic links and faster multi-page I/O with xfstests now running in CI, PVH boot support and running as a Firecracker microVM guest, and TDX boot work split across all vCPUs because every page must be accepted before use; virtualisation support in OSTD following RFC-0003's split where OSTD owns the mechanism (virtualisation hardware state, second-stage address translation, the guest-host switch) and the kernel owns the policy (VM and vCPU lifecycle, memory slots, interrupt chips, device emulation and eventually a KVM-compatible /dev/kvm), delivering the Intel VMX foundation and documented by a Book example that writes a minimal hypervisor in about 100 lines of safe Rust over three abstractions, with the stated motivation that Xen-style type-1 hypervisors depend on a full dom0 Linux for drivers while Linux with KVM puts a large C kernel in every VM's trusted base; a Rust-native device model in the new aster-device component where the type system enforces what Linux enforces by convention (a Driver<B> can only register on bus B, a ClassDevice<C> carries its class in its type so a ClassObserver<C> only hears about class C devices and can never be handed a terminal, and an Attr<D> is declared against device type D with callbacks receiving &D so no callback has to downcast a generic device pointer); an AI code review skill whose framing is that agents make code cheap while human review remains the bottleneck, built on Coding Guidelines reorganised around five reviewer personas into 81 guidelines with stable short names, running one pass per persona, attempting to refute each comment before keeping it, and optimised against a benchmark of 58 review problems with 138 expected defects mined almost entirely from Asterinas's own history where every miss drives a change to the guidelines or the skill; and self-hosting, where Asterinas NixOS boots in a VM, the repository is cloned inside it, the Nix dev shell is entered, make kernel runs and the fresh kernel boots in a nested QEMU VM with Nix, Cargo, rustc and QEMU all running on Asterinas, which the announcement calls one of the largest real-world workloads the kernel has been put through, alongside a new Nix flake with toolchain, QEMU and firmware prebuilt on Cachix. Closes by arguing framekernel's real contribution is turning security into a measurable budget, that the most convincing maturity signals are the references to third-party test suites (doubling xfstests overlayfs cases, xfstests in CI for virtio-fs) rather than feature lists, that the AI review skill generalises a problem every AI-accelerated project now faces and is smartest in requiring each subjective comment to cite a guideline and in mining its benchmark from project history, that the near-term landing zone is more likely guest kernel for VM-based containers than replacing Linux generally given narrower requirements and a strong need for a small memory-safe trusted base, and that this release belongs to a pattern of decisions about where to draw boundaries rather than about being stronger.
  - Key topics: Asterinas, Rust OS kernel, framekernel, framework and services, unsafe Rust, OSTD, OSDK, safe Rust, monolithic kernel, microkernel, address space, memory safety, trusted computing base, DRM, aster-drm, GEM dumb buffers, KMS, Xorg, Mesa, software OpenGL, fbdev, AArch64, GICv3, PL031 RTC, PL011 UART, virtio-mmio, vDSO, Tier 2 platform, LoongArch, RISC-V, Kata Containers, Confidential Containers, overlayfs, xfstests, mount propagation, fsopen, virtio-fs, O_DIRECT, PVH, Firecracker, Intel TDX, VMX, VMCS, EPT, RFC-0003, KVM, /dev/kvm, hypervisor, aster-device, devtmpfs, class device, sysfs attributes, AI code review, Coding Guidelines, self-hosting, Nix flake, Cachix, MPL-2.0, 译文

- [Linus 用 Claude Code 改内核：这份 commit message 比那个性能数字更值得读](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-10-12_linus-torvalds-claude-code-kernel/): Translation+analysis of two Phoronix reports about Linus Torvalds using Claude Code for Linux kernel work, read against the primary sources (the commit message and the git tag). Covers the branch noref-filemap-read-with-llm in torvalds/linux.git and commit 4c0f3697118eb3a708ea79175f7f07c43339bfab, whose goal is reading from the page cache without folio references, and reproduces Torvalds's own AI disclosure verbatim: the code, the test programs, the review behind the list and the first draft of the text were done with an LLM coding assistant (Claude Code) under his direction, while the measurements were run on his machine. Explains the problem in his words (small reads of one file from many threads contend on the folio refcount because filemap_get_read_batch takes a reference with lock cmpxchg and filemap_read drops it with lock decl, so every read writes the struct page line twice; Matthew raised it in 2024 from a customer workload) and the reported measurement on his laptop (i7-8565U, 4 cores / 8 threads, where that line takes 99.92 percent of load HITMs for 8 threads doing 16-byte pread of one page). Sets out the idea (a folio removed from the page cache returns to the allocator only after an RCU grace period, so a page found by xas_load under rcu_read_lock holds the file's data until rcu_read_unlock and filemap_read can copy straight to the user buffer with page faults disabled, requiring no reference, no on-stack bounce buffer, no seqcount, no post-copy check and no read size limit) and the crucial framing that deferring the free eliminates the failure cases rather than detecting them, listing what earlier attempts could not see (free, reuse and re-insert at the same index; migration since __folio_migrate_mapping does not use page_cache_delete; and reading memory that is no longer page cache at all, including secretmem, unaccepted memory and MMIO with undesired read effects), plus Matthew's objection that it feels too risky to have so much memory waiting to be reused, which the commit itself names as the least solved part. Reproduces the performance table and the costs: 8 threads going from 2937-2975 to 725-726 kernel cycles per read and from 9.9-10.4M to 30-33M reads per second, load HITM falling from 30538 to 101, but a single-threaded read into a not-present user page rising from roughly 4117-4188 to 6543-6593 cycles; notes the measurement caveats (his laptop only, ext4, mitigations and CONFIG_HARDENED_USERCOPY off, hardware throttling so cost per read is the comparable figure, and the statement that machines with more cores or sockets should gain more but nothing bigger was measured). Covers the testing section and its honest limits: evict-race with four readers verifying every byte against a thread evicting and immediately reusing pages produced 0 bad reads in 30-second runs of about 10^8 reads, while a debug patch that frees PG_rcu_free pages immediately produced 12 and 138 bad reads, so the test does detect a broken guarantee; and the flat statement that those tests, one gcc build of one x86-64 config and running the laptop on it are all the testing there is, with no lockdep, no CONFIG_DEBUG_ATOMIC_SLEEP and no KASAN. Explains the known problem the commit leaves in the open: the allocator cannot see the waiting pages because they have refcount 0, are not PageBuddy, and sit on no pcp list or counter, which once ran a machine out of memory; the 1024-page limit is called a guess; and with no idle CPU an average of 177 MiB waits with peaks of 870 MiB. Notes the new contract this creates (a lockless reader relying on the deferral must hold a reference to mapping->host, which an open file does) and what is deliberately not deferred (folios of an inode with I_FREEING, plus hugetlb and the swap cache). Then covers the same-day assoc-array-fixes tag, where Torvalds writes that a reported assoc_array bug and its patch were too obscure for him to follow so he did what he preaches and used modern LLM tools: an LLM-assisted branch that splits up large hard-to-read functions, then run through a user-space test harness which confirmed the reported bug and found three more, all going back to the 2013 commit that first added the library. Closes by reading the commit message as a technical writing template (Problem, Idea, Design decisions, Numbers with costs and measurement caveats, Testing with a falsification control, Known problems inviting specific eyes), arguing his AI disclosure is valuable because it separates what the AI did from what the human did, contrasting this with the kernel networking maintainers' demand that contributors take responsibility for thinking, and noting that the branch name itself leaves a permanent label in git history.
  - Key topics: Linus Torvalds, Claude Code, Linux kernel, noref-filemap-read-with-llm, folio references, page cache, filemap_get_read_batch, filemap_read, lock cmpxchg, lock decl, struct page, load HITM, perf c2c, RCU grace period, rcu_read_lock, xas_load, secretmem, unaccepted memory, MMIO, folio migration, PG_rcu_free, queue_rcu_work, kfree_rcu, should_reclaim_retry, NR_FREE_PAGES, KASAN, lockdep, assoc_array, assoc-array-fixes, LLM-assisted development, AI disclosure, 译文

- [红帽的混沌工程复盘：四个客户案例里，我最在意的是「保存实验」这一条](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-10-12_red-hat-chaos-engineering-lessons/): Translation+analysis of a Red Hat blog post by Naga Ravi Chaitanya Elluri (chaos engineering lead for OpenShift and managed services) drawing lessons from four anonymised enterprise engagements with Krkn and Krkn Operator. Frames the opening claim that resilience is a business requirement because failed transactions interrupt revenue, infrastructure outages affect multiple workloads, database failures put critical data at risk, and repeated failures erode customer trust in a way that can outlast the outage, then lays out the chain from business need to SLO (internal measurable targets) to SLA (customer commitments and consequences) to chaos experiments as the mechanism that tests whether the commitment actually holds. Presents the four cases in a table mapping injected failures to exposed defects: a latency-sensitive trading application on ROSA tested against availability-zone outages, compute-node failures, Amazon Aurora outages, API throttling and storage exhaustion, which surfaced reliability and performance bottlenecks earlier testing missed; an institution migrating virtualised workloads to OpenShift Virtualization where simultaneous control-plane and worker-node loss plus storage disruption and DNS outages led to VirtIO driver fixes, OpenShift Data Foundation tuning, I/O limits, fencing improvements and better alerts, with storage recovery reported within seconds and no VM crashes in validated scenarios; relational databases tested against full disks, split-brain-capable network partitions and abrupt loss of active compute nodes, leading platform engineers and database architects to tune storage classes and IOPS limits for crash recovery; and a financial-services payment environment using a hub-and-spoke model with GitOps to coordinate network packet loss and CPU exhaustion experiments alongside recurring GameDays, reporting improved recovery times through repeated drills and joint root cause analysis. Extracts each case's verification principle (put recovery evidence into the launch decision with SLOs aligned to customer SLAs and explicit recovery limits; validate recovery from the application's perspective under representative load, traffic patterns and network topology because one infrastructure failure disrupts many business services; make data integrity a recovery requirement by starting from recovery-time and data-loss objectives and then choosing failures that could violate them, judging storage tuning by its effect on recovery rather than only normal performance; and follow the transaction through to completion, tracing a request through the application, dependencies, database and final confirmation and checking retries, duplicate processing and recovery time to reveal customer impact that infrastructure health alone misses), and highlights the advice to include partial failures such as intermittent packet loss and slow responses while watching for growing queues, excessive retries and failures spreading between services. Then argues the three closing lessons in reverse priority order, putting save and replay workflows first: a one-off exercise yields a snapshot while replaying validated experiments on every release and configuration change yields a trend line and catches regressions before rollout, and the requirement that transaction, data-integrity and recovery checks pass alongside the resilience score guards against the metric detaching from the service outcome it is meant to measure. Also recommends validating the team's response alongside system recovery by naming a recovery owner per exercise, measuring response times, improving alerts and runbooks, and repeating the exercise to verify the improvements. Closes with a concrete starting sequence (write the SLO before the experiment, pick a scenario where one dependency failing interrupts a customer journey rather than the easiest failure to inject, observe application and infrastructure layers simultaneously, assign a recovery owner and require specific work items rather than a report, re-run after fixes, then commit the experiment to version control and attach it to the release process) and notes the method is tool-independent even though Krkn provides the reusable-workflow capability.

- [解锁 Bootloader 不等于 Root：Android 刷机链的每一层到底在解什么锁](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-10-11_android-bootloader-unlock-root-chain/): Original analysis separating bootloader unlocking from root acquisition on Android, grounded in AOSP documentation and the official docs of each rooting solution, and correcting a widespread but inaccurate description of how Magisk works. Establishes the precise AVB semantics first: Android Verified Boot 2.0 defines LOCKED as meaning verification errors are fatal and UNLOCKED as meaning they are not, so unlocking downgrades the consequence of a verification failure rather than disabling verification, and the device still reports its boot state as unlocked or orange. Distinguishes the bootloader's own chain-of-trust signature checks from AVB's vbmeta descriptors (a hash descriptor for boot, a hashtree descriptor for system, and a kernel-cmdline descriptor that sets up dm-verity) and from dm-verity's block-level hash tree verification at mount time. Covers the two hard constraints AVB places on state transitions (physical presence must be asserted, and transitioning from UNLOCKED back to LOCKED requires a data wipe where full-disk encryption is required) and explains why unlocking necessarily wipes data: encryption key protection is bound to the verified boot state, so without the wipe unlocking would become a physical-access data extraction channel. Notes the alternative path of flashing a custom AVB key on devices that support an avb_custom_key partition, which lets you sign your own images and relock, at the cost of failing official OTA verification and bricking the device if the key is lost. Then explains why root is a separate construction rather than a switch: Android's isolation rests on Linux UID/GID, application sandboxes and SEAndroid, in which even system daemons are confined to UIDs like system, radio and shell and cannot rewrite read-only partitions that dm-verity verifies at mount. Traces why the traditional approach of dropping a su binary into /system/xbin no longer works (System-as-Root, dynamic partitions and dm-verity together), which is why modern solutions are systemless, overlaying or bind-mounting content during early boot before write protection takes effect, and why that requires patching a boot image, which in turn requires an unlocked bootloader. Explains the init_boot split introduced by AOSP: from Android 12 the generic boot image (GKI) contains the generic ramdisk and the GKI kernel, while devices launching with Android 13 move the generic ramdisk into a separate init_boot partition, leaving boot with only the kernel, so the correct patch target is boot.img before Android 13 and init_boot.img on devices that shipped with Android 13 or later - a common cause of flashing failures. Presents a chain diagram whose key feature is that flashing a third-party ROM and acquiring root are independent branches, since custom ROMs like LineageOS ship unrooted by design. Compares the three main rooting approaches with their real mechanisms and prerequisites: Magisk patching the boot or init_boot ramdisk and replacing /init with magiskinit to take control as PID 1 during early boot, with magic mount (tmpfs bind mounts) as its core filesystem mechanism and OverlayFS available on newer kernels, being the most compatible option with the largest module ecosystem and having removed bundled MagiskHide since Magisk 24 in favour of Zygisk and DenyList; KernelSU working in kernel mode to grant root directly in kernel space with a kernel interface that can set hardware breakpoints on any process, access physical memory invisibly and intercept any syscall, requiring kernel source or a GKI kernel and delegating mounting to metamodules such as meta-overlayfs for flexibility and reduced detection surface; and APatch patching the kernel image directly via KernelPatch with SELinux bypassed via hook rather than modified in context, requiring only a stock boot.img and no kernel source, limited to ARM64, kernels 3.18 to 6.12 and CONFIG_KALLSYMS, incompatible with Knox-protected Samsung hardware, and able to root a thread within an app's own context without libsu or IPC. Then lays out the costs that cannot be engineered around: the unlocked state is recorded and reported, Keymaster/Keymint reports the device as Unlocked, and all device-integrity-based checks fail. Details the Play Integrity tiers (MEETS_BASIC_INTEGRITY mainly indicating a physical Android device, passing even with an unlocked bootloader; MEETS_DEVICE_INTEGRITY requiring on Android 13 and later a locked bootloader and a certified OEM image, reinforced by Google to require a hardware-backed positive verified boot verdict; and MEETS_STRONG_INTEGRITY generally considered unachievable on an unlocked device) and makes the key distinction that hiding measures can defeat an app's observation of root but cannot change the hardware-backed conclusion that the device state is unlocked. Covers the Widevine consequence (many devices drop from L1 to L3 after unlocking, sometimes recoverable by relocking, device-dependent, because L1 requires a trust chain extending from a secure bootloader and keybox writing only in the locked state), the expanded attack surface (the privilege channel is itself a kernel-level backdoor whose authorization layer may be bypassed, contrasted with APatch's SuperKey and KernelSU's in-kernel verification as attempts to move authorization earlier), and the changed data-security model for a lost unlocked device. Closes with a comparison table across layer, problem solved, essential action, whether the permission model changes, whether device integrity is affected and whether each can exist alone, plus the framing that unlocking grants no new permission but converts 'the system refuses you' into 'the system permits the change and keeps accounts'. Appends official links for Magisk (repository and documentation), KernelSU (site and source), APatch (FAQ and source), KernelPatch, LineageOS downloads and wiki and browser flash tool, TWRP, Android SDK Platform Tools, AOSP AVB and generic boot partition documentation, Play Integrity documentation, and XDA Forums, with a warning that look-alike download sites for KernelSU and APatch are common vectors for backdoored rooting tools.
  - Key topics: Android, bootloader unlock, root, Android Verified Boot, AVB, vbmeta, dm-verity, LOCKED and UNLOCKED, chain of trust, physical presence, data wipe, avb_custom_key, System-as-Root, dynamic partitions, systemless, magic mount, init hijacking, magiskinit, Zygisk, DenyList, MagiskHide removal, KernelSU, metamodule, meta-overlayfs, GKI, APatch, KernelPatch, SuperKey, KPM, ARM64, CONFIG_KALLSYMS, Knox, SELinux, SEAndroid, UID root, TEE, TrustZone, Keymaster, Keymint, Play Integrity API, MEETS_BASIC_INTEGRITY, MEETS_DEVICE_INTEGRITY, MEETS_STRONG_INTEGRITY, SafetyNet deprecation, Widevine L1 L3, hardware-backed attestation, init_boot, boot.img, LineageOS, TWRP, fastboot, adb, platform-tools, XDA, 原创

- [用 Claude 造 Office 替代品：ROADMAP 自己写着完成度约 50%，而仓库里的 CLAUDE.md 才是重点](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-10-11_artcraft-office-clones-claude/): Analysis of ArtCraft's Microsoft Office replacements (WordCraft, GridCraft, DeckCraft) read from the repositories rather than the press coverage, with all repository metrics measured via the GitHub API on 11 October 2026. Establishes that ArtCraft's code lives under the storytold GitHub organisation (created January 2021, 56 public repositories, getartcraft.com) and that this is a suite of eleven applications, not three: photocraft at 44,858 stars, artcraft at 15,999, lightcraft 9,554, filmcraft 9,311, pdfcraft 8,703, vectorcraft 6,632, wordcraft 4,112, gridcraft 2,195, cadcraft 2,196, soundcraft 1,528 and craft-launcher 838, with the Adobe batch created on 30 September 2026 and the Office batch on 7 October, and per-release download counts (WordCraft v0.5.0 36,955; GridCraft v0.5.0 28,955; DeckCraft v0.5.0 23,612) showing real demand. Details the clean-room boundary (competitor software may be observed black-box by running it with synthetic files and screenshotting by window id into a gitignored plan directory, but nothing inside the application bundle may be read, disassembled or copied, files produced by it may never be committed, and GPL/AGPL/LGPL code from LibreOffice, Gnumeric, AbiWord or pandoc may never be copied, with behaviour taken from public specifications ECMA-376/ISO 29500, the RTF spec and ODF 1.3), the absolute asset rule (no vendor iconography, images, artwork, fonts, templates, themes, clip art, cursors or sounds ever, not even temporarily; prefer art drawn in code; every asset needs a row in ATTRIBUTION.md enforced by a CI check; proprietary fonts never bundled and documents requesting Calibri, Aptos or Cambria rendered with system fonts or metric-compatible open substitutes), the 'Never crash' section (no unwrap/expect/panic/todo/unimplemented and unsafe_code forbidden in non-test code, errors as Result with ?, input-derived numbers treated as hostile with bounded allocations for REPT, SEQUENCE and whole-column references, bounded recursion, a Session::execute last-resort guard described explicitly as a safety net and not a licence, regression tests required for every crash fix and clippy lints denied at crate level), and the 'everything is a command' architecture (every user-visible behaviour is a command with id, label, ribbon path, shortcut, parameter documentation and tests, ids following Excel's ribbon, with the control channel, CLI and MCP all reaching the same commands, and programmatic calls never opening dialogs) which simultaneously delivers testability, agent control and auditable permissions. Notes the parallel-agent workflow rules (separate CARGO_TARGET_DIR per agent, edit only the crates you own, one task id per commit), the instruction for UI work to look at the snapshot PNG and compare it with the observed-UI record, and the gitignored plan directory separating agent context from published code. Explains the licence reasoning: existing open-source office suites are MPL/LGPL family, so copying their implementation would prevent MIT/Apache-2.0 release, which is why the project takes the harder road of rebuilding from public specifications plus black-box observation, buying commercial freedom at the cost of walking the entire format-compatibility long tail itself - which is offered as the main explanation for the 50 percent figure rather than any limitation of AI capability. Flags one gap: the CLAUDE.md files repeatedly cite storytold/craftrules as the authority for shared standards (never-crash, fonts, test corpora, progress docs) but that repository returns 404 and is not public, contrasted with the previous day's finding that the Veda repository declares nothing about how it was developed while this one documents it elaborately. Closes with practical guidance by scenario (worth installing for individuals and Linux desktop users, strongest selling point being agent automation via MCP, CLI and the command architecture; avoid for enterprises with VBA macros and complex templates given VBA is out of scope, round-trip compatibility is unverified, localisation is at 10 percent and the project is alpha), and the judgement that the CLAUDE.md is the genuinely new artefact here, that the 50 percent reflects a legal route choice rather than a capability ceiling, and that the project places AI as an external agent controlling the application rather than an in-app assistant, solving testability, agent control and auditability together.

- [LineageOS 24 一次把 174 个设备搬上 Android 17：而它同时宣布了一条硬底线](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-10-11_lineageos-24-changelog-32/): Translation+analysis of LineageOS Changelog 32 (Nolen Johnson, 11 October 2026), covering the 24.0 branch rebased onto Android 17 and notably early this year because previous efforts adapting to Google's heavy refactoring made the rebase faster than anticipated. Reports the device counts the author counted row by row from the build roster tables since the original gives no totals: 174 devices moved to 24.0, six to 23.2 and five to 22.2, spanning the latest Pixel 10 family (frankel, blazer, mustang, rango, stallion) down to Pixel 4-era hardware plus Motorola, OnePlus, Sony, Xiaomi, Samsung and a set of gaming handhelds (AYN Odin 2, Retroid Pocket 6, Razer Edge 5G), along with less commonly discussed devices such as the Amazon Fire Max 11 and Solana Saga. Highlights the hard line the project announced: even though devices on Linux kernel 4.4 and 4.9 have been ported to 23.2 and 24.0, only 22.2 submissions are accepted for them because those kernels carry countless hacky platform commits that are difficult to carry forward, while 22.2 keeps receiving monthly builds and security patches until Google stops distributing official security bulletins for Android 15 and new 22.2 devices can still be submitted - framing this as layering rather than abandonment. Also covers the new threshold for 23.2 and 24.0, that only kernels with 1:1 eBPF backports, that build fully without GCC, and with many other important backported features are shipped, and reads it as a requirement for kernels aligned with upstream rather than merely bootable ones, connecting it to the 4.4/4.9 freeze as a consequence of fork depth. Details the security patch status (patches from August 2025 to October 2026 merged across 18.1 through 24.0; the security patch level string only updated on 21/Android 14 and newer where Google distributes attestable bulletins, while 18.1, 19.1 and 20.0 continue to be backported without changing the string; legacy 15.1, 16.0 and 17.1 patched through November 2025 with the December 2025 bulletins containing difficult patches the project could not adapt), praising the specificity and the honesty about what can and cannot be claimed. Covers the browser-based WebUSB flash tools for ADB, Fastboot, the Amlogic burn protocol and Samsung's Odin protocol, stressing that they do not replace the Wiki guides which remain the default and supported path, noting the browser requirements (Chrome or Edge, USB drivers on Windows, udev rules on Linux except on distributions with systemd v261 or newer) and the troubleshooting advice to avoid hubs, extensions and adapters, and crediting the upstream fastboot.js, ya-webadb and libmjolnir projects. Also covers the new Canvas image editor pairing with Glimpse and Aperture, the Updater redesign with streamed updates by default to cut A/B installation times and automatic recovery partition updates on non-A/B devices on the boot after a successful update, Catapult battery indicators, Twelve's fixes for tracks getting stuck with offload enabled and improved Jellyfin support, Jelly's PWA-like shortcut support, the SetupWizard rewrite with device-specific hooks, WebView 155.0.8059.30, and the practice of sending fixes back upstream for Etar and Seedvault. Covers the CI/CD work (CI+1/CI-1 votes running pre-commit, lint and clang-format checks and REUSE licence compliance checks, and CD pushing APKs on merge), the end-to-end accessibility audit performed free of charge by the a11y project with recovery navigation and UI already reworked and free training given to over 40 contributors, the migration of Samsung devices on the Wiki from ODIN and Heimdall to samloader-rs, the commonisation of legacy device shims into android_hardware_lineage_compat, the 14 common SoC kernels spanning MSM8996 to SM8850, the generic targets for emulator, GSI, Cuttlefish and QEMU, and the experimental bare-metal generic target reported to boot on common x86_64 PCs, Apple Silicon Macs, NVIDIA DGX Spark and Qualcomm Snapdragon X Series laptops. Notes the tenth anniversary on 24 December 2026, the project being the first third-party Android distribution with complete Welsh language support, and closes by arguing the real news is the calibration: the three-layer treatment by kernel generation is more responsible than cutting old devices off and more sustainable than propping everything up, that it only works because the older branches still receive security patches, and that the device count reflects hundreds of maintainers each carrying a few devices forward rather than a company funding the work.
  - Key topics: LineageOS, LineageOS 24.0, Android 17, AOSP, build roster, maintainer-driven project, kernel 4.4, kernel 4.9, LineageOS 22.2, 23.2, eBPF backports, GCC-free builds, Clang, GKI, security patch level, attestable bulletins, legacy branches, WebUSB, flash.lineageos.org, fastboot.js, ya-webadb, libmjolnir, Odin protocol, Amlogic burn mode, samloader-rs, Heimdall, Canvas, Glimpse, Aperture, Updater, streamed updates, A/B partitions, Virtual A/B, dynamic partitions, Catapult, Twelve, Jelly, Jellyfin, SetupWizard, WebView, Seedvault, Etar, REUSE compliance, pre-commit, clang-format, CI/CD, accessibility audit, a11y project, SoC common kernels, android_hardware_lineage_compat, shims, generic targets, GSI, Cuttlefish, QEMU, libvirt, UTM, bare-metal generic target, DGX Spark, Snapdragon X, Welsh Cymraeg, 译文

- [「很难」是过去时：一个人 8 天写出微内核操作系统，以及为什么 unikernel 又回来了](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-10-11_unikernels-veda-agentic-os/): Combined translation+analysis of Geoffrey Huntley's conversation with Justin Cormack (an early MirageOS developer) arguing that unikernels were hard, key word were, because those hard concepts now live in the model weights and only the cognitive dogma remains, read alongside the Veda repository as a concrete data point. Covers Huntley's definition of a unikernel (your application is the operating system, no userland, nothing to fork or spawn, so a web server or DNS or email must be written as libraries), Cormack's recollection of the original friction (Mirage had TCP and HTTPS stacks but almost nothing for storage, pulling drivers out of NetBSD to run in userspace), and the design-debt argument that every non-unikernel application assumes an application with an operating system underneath, that the multi-user operating system exists because a human operator sat in front of it forty years ago, and that this is design debt which matters now because popping a userland application yields a shell that acts as a VIP butler service for exfiltration; in a unikernel the attack surface is smaller because functionality absent from the application does not exist, so there is no next hop, and with no shell or interpreter there is nothing in the model weights that knows what to do next, turning a drive-by RCE into a targeted attack requiring source code. Also preserves Cormack's fair pushback that attack-surface reduction is something people are very fuzzy about since almost every Linux environment still has something effectively equivalent to an interpreter, that programs can be executed without a writable filesystem, and that memory safety and gadgets remain concerns, along with Huntley's counter that we have spent twenty-six years chipping away at attack surface since the don't-put-the-compiler-on-production era, build versus production containers and Chainguard, without ever going the other direction to ensure there is no attack surface at all. Describes the porting thesis that with a golden oracle porting is a loop, illustrated by Cormack having an agent write mkfs.xfs in Rust producing byte-for-byte identical output with every flag interpreted and tests across block sizes in a few hours, notes the S3-for-everything storage recommendation, the seL4-or-unikernels security fork, and the observation that a KVM (essentially Firecracker) escape that week collected only 50,000 USD despite being able to root every managed cloud provider. Then presents Veda (github.com/vahmoh25/Veda, GPL-3.0) with metrics measured via the GitHub API on 11 October 2026: created 3 October 2026, 192 commits in 8 days, a single contributor, 677 first-party Rust source files totalling 8.86 MB, 1,171 files, 56 stars, 6 forks and zero releases, covering everything written from scratch including the UEFI loader, a capability-based microkernel called vkernel, drivers, system services, the window system, the vui toolkit and applications, with the driver, filesystem, window system and agent running as user-space processes supervised by init. Details the features claimed (compositing window manager with server-side decorations and GPU composition via OpenGL ES on Intel graphics, user-space networking and WPA2/WPA3 Wi-Fi, TLS 1.3/1.2 through vtls, an echo-cancelling audio service, disks driven natively with all other devices taken from Linux running in a driver VM on Veda's own VMX+EPT hypervisor with DMA confined and interrupts remapped by a self-written IOMMU driver, virtio-blk/AHCI/NVMe with crash-safe snapshots, three 3D games, OpenGL ES 3.0 with a multithreaded software renderer fallback at 75 fps under QEMU, GCC 16 running inside Veda with C programs as musl static ELF going through vposix, a POSIX layer written in Rust) and the agentic design: the agent is a system service started at boot and restarted on failure, applications describe actions with typed parameters and a risk level and report structured state and execute through the same code as keyboard and mouse so there is no screen scraping or simulated clicks, with more than 70 actions across built-in applications, every action classified routine, sensitive or destructive, and consent enforced by the agent service rather than the language model with the call held until the user answers, only the desktop shell able to answer, and nothing the agent reads able to approve anything. Contrasts the two directions, noting that Huntley's core security argument is that a shell should lead nowhere while Veda ships a terminal and GCC 16, so unikernels delete while agentic operating systems add, and that the intersection is likely system-level enforcement outside the model's output. Flags the notable gap that the repository contains no statement anywhere about whether AI was used in its development, with every AI mention in the README referring to the built-in agent rather than the writing of the code, and observes that the silence is misplaced given that Huntley's thesis would welcome the former explanation, while listing the honest caveats that the project is eight days old with zero releases, that real-hardware use requires UEFI with Secure Boot off and VT-x plus VT-d, and that being able to run is not the same as being maintainable.
  - Key topics: unikernels, MirageOS, Justin Cormack, Geoffrey Huntley, seL4, design debt, attack surface reduction, shell as exfiltration butler, prompt injection, model weights, porting with an oracle, mkfs.xfs in Rust, S3 for everything, KVM escape, Firecracker, Veda, agentic-native operating system, vkernel, capability-based microkernel, driver VM, VMX, EPT, IOMMU, virtio-blk, AHCI, NVMe, OpenGL ES 3.0, GLSL ES, Deepgram Voice Agent, vposix, GCC 16, musl, agent consent, routine sensitive destructive, Vahid Mohammadi, 译文

- [SQLite 3.54 终于放弃 Windows XP：一个数据库引擎的兼容性债，还了二十多年](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-10-09_sqlite-3-54-released/): Translation+analysis of SQLite 3.54.0, released 9 October 2026, whose headline change is dropping support for Windows XP and earlier, including Windows CE, raising the floor to Windows Vista. Explains why that is more than housekeeping: because the minimum version rose, SQLite can implement non-recursive mutexes on Windows with Slim Reader/Writer Locks instead of CriticalSection, which the official release notes list as a performance improvement, making the platform drop and the speedup two ends of the same causality - compatibility code does not cost a few extra branches but forces a heavier underlying mechanism on a hot path. Covers the performance figures with their limits: about 4 percent faster than the previous release and about 7.5 percent faster than 3.51 a year earlier on the official Speedtest benchmark, but measured on Linux x64 so the Windows SRWL gains are not reflected in those numbers, and with the candid official note that it does not mean every application using SQLite gets correspondingly faster since results depend on how the database is used, meaning the only reliable test is your own workload. Lists the CLI improvements (columnar output modes now showing the column-name header by default even when a query returns no rows; the new --ifmt and --fpfmt options for printf-style control of integer and floating-point rendering; --rowcount on; --titles always becoming the default with legacy behaviour restorable via -titles on; the .diskused dot-command replacing the now-deprecated standalone sqlite3_analyzer utility; prompt strings supporting escape sequences that expand to state information and reading SQLITE_PS1 and SQLITE_PS2; NO_COLOR honoured by the default prompt; -csv automatically disabling display limits; and Unix preserving zero bytes when outputting unformatted BLOB values), the query planner improvements (better optimization of expr OR TRUE and expr OR FALSE, ignoring DISTINCT on the right-hand side of IN, faster and less memory-hungry UNION queries with a LIMIT of exactly 1, and not touching an expression index during UPDATE when the indexed value is unchanged), O_TMPFILE for temporary files where supported, date/time additions (the weekday -N form and the end of modifier), new interfaces (sqlite3_result_str, sqlite3_incomplete, SQLITE_LIMIT_SCHEMA and SQLITE_LIMIT_TRIGGER_STEPS) and the %J and %j printf conversions for rendering JSON string literals. Flags the single potential incompatibility the release notes mark themselves, that ALTER TABLE no longer allows adding, dropping or renaming columns named ROWID, _ROWID_ or OID. Closes with a general framework for evaluating decisions to drop old platform support: do not just count user share but ask which layer the cost lands on, treat costs on shared hot paths as continuous and universal, prefer cutting the minimum version over keeping a compile-time switch that forces two paths to be maintained and tested forever, and announce a migration window while stating the concrete capability or performance gained rather than only what was abandoned.
  - Key topics: SQLite, SQLite 3.54, embedded database, Windows XP, Windows CE, Windows Vista, Slim Reader/Writer Locks, SRWL, CriticalSection, mutexes, amalgamation, speedtest benchmark, query planner, expression indexes, OR TRUE optimization, IN DISTINCT, UNION LIMIT 1, O_TMPFILE, ALTER TABLE ROWID, sqlite3_analyzer, diskused, SQLITE_PS1, NO_COLOR, weekday modifier, end of modifier, sqlite3_result_str, sqlite3_incomplete, SQLITE_LIMIT_SCHEMA, compatibility debt, platform support lifecycle, 译文

- [LTS 在 AI 时代过时了？补丁洪流是真的，但「改用滚动发布」是个假二选一](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-10-10_lts-vs-rolling-release-genai/): Translation+analysis of Qualcomm engineer Khem Raj's Linux Plumbers Conference 2026 talk 'Relevance of LTS distro releases and the GenAI world', in which he asks whether LTS distributions still make sense now that GenAI coding agents are increasing both patch volume and package upgrade cadence, predicting the maintenance load on LTS will rise dramatically over the next two to three years and suggesting rolling releases may be more viable, particularly for embedded distributions like Yocto and buildroot with small communities. It quotes his abstract verbatim (including coding agents already generating patches for package upgrades and handling CI/CD in Yocto and other distributions, his proposal to use GenAI tooling to help maintain LTS releases, and his own admission that rolling releases present certification and qualification challenges) and notes his focus is embedded and small-community distributions rather than enterprise server deployments. Then adds the corroborating evidence he did not present, drawn from the kernel community's 2026 record: networking maintainer Jakub Kicinski reporting that he and Paolo merged a very similar number of net (632) and net-next (648) patches in one cycle with one third to one half of the net-next patches seeming like AI-driven low-priority fixes, cleanups and clarifications, stating 'we are completely overwhelmed', and noting that Meta provided sufficient LLM budget and access to run reviews with multiple frontier models on each patch while conceding LLMs can only do so much in review and that long-racy APIs for rare events like PCIe errors and timeouts can no longer be ignored because LLMs keep finding them; the diversion of over 50 fixes to net-next for Linux 7.4 rather than squeezing them into 7.3 with the comment 'pretty sure you won't be impressed by the size of this PR but this is after we shaved off 50 fixes'; and the institutional countermeasures: the kernel staging area rejecting AI/LLM-generated patches except genuine security fixes, wireless maintainer Johannes Berg's three-second review rule and his explicit refusal to argue with an LLM that can bullshit out code faster than email can deliver it (quoting his analysis of a patch that implemented the same validation in multiple branches of the same switch statement, where the human in the loop should have stepped back to ask what the code's semantics should be), syzbot disabled for sending AI-assisted patches to the wireless subsystem, NetworkManager's canary word 'biblioklept' planted in AGENTS.md to flag AI agents that follow instructions (with the observation that this only catches compliant agents), and AF_ALG restrictions in Linux 7.3 justified by a security and maintenance nightmare. Argues the conclusion is a false dichotomy because the bottleneck is review bandwidth rather than backporting, and rolling releases merely move the queue from downstream backporting to upstream review, which is the part that has already broken; identifies three better questions (how to expand review bandwidth, including the meta-approach of using LLMs to review LLM patches that both Raj and Kicinski are pursuing, how to set rules, and who should be allowed to submit), highlights Berg's distinction between a narrow test-passing fix and a correct abstraction as the most transferable lesson for anyone writing code with AI assistance, advises against migrating enterprise deployments to rolling releases since predictability, rollback and compliance evidence are exactly where LTS wins while the faster-security-fix advantage is often offset by change risk, and closes with the optimistic note that AI-generated patches surface long-standing races in rare code paths, meaning the noise also carries information at a high price.

- [三条来自 LWN 的时间线：Python 3.15、Let's Encrypt 的 64 天证书、systemd 的自我交代](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-10-09_lwn-python-315-letsencrypt-systemd/): Combined translation+analysis of three LWN.net briefs published on 9 October 2026, read as three timelines of different scale. For Python 3.15 (released 9 October), it organizes the release by PEP: PEP 814 adding the frozendict builtin (not a dict subclass, inheriting directly from object, hashable when all keys and values are hashable, preserving insertion order while comparison ignores order), PEP 661 adding the sentinel builtin (preserving identity when copied, usable in type expressions with the pipe operator, pickleable when importable by module and name), PEP 686 making UTF-8 the default encoding independently of the system environment, PEP 810 explicit lazy imports, PEP 829 package startup configuration files, PEP 799 adding a dedicated profiling package and the Tachyon high-frequency statistical sampling profiler with sampling rates up to 1,000,000 Hz plus gil and exception modes, PEP 831 enabling frame pointers by default for system-level observability, PEP 798 unpacking in comprehensions, PEP 803/820/793 adding a stable ABI for free-threaded builds, and various typing and C API changes; it flags the easily missed migration trap that import lines in .pth files are silently deprecated and ignored when a matching .start file exists while sys.path extension lines are unaffected, and reports the JIT figures of 8 to 9 percent geometric mean improvement on x86-64 Linux over the standard interpreter and 12 to 13 percent on AArch64 macOS over the tail-calling interpreter, alongside Windows 64-bit binaries now using the tail-calling interpreter and macOS binaries installing free-threading support by default. For Let's Encrypt, it reproduces the official timeline (staging issues 64-day certificates from 14 October 2026, the default drops to 64 days on 10 February 2027, the last 90-day certificate expires on 11 May 2027, lifetimes fall to 45 days on 16 February 2028, and industry rules cap lifetimes at 47 days from 15 March 2029) together with the authorization reuse period shrinking from 30 days to 10 days and then to 7 hours, explains that the reuse cut exists to comply with the 2029 rules and to eliminate CAA rechecking for validation data older than seven hours, notes the reassuring points that no valid certificates will be revoked and that nothing changes if validation reuse was never deliberately relied upon, and turns the official advice into an operations checklist: grep cron jobs, wrapper scripts and runbooks for hardcoded numbers like 83, 80 or 60, renew at roughly two thirds of the lifetime instead, confirm the ACME client implements ARI, treat manual renewal as the real risk since 64 days means about every two months and 45 days about every six weeks, and avoid assuming the February 2027 date applies to other certificate authorities. For systemd, it states upfront that The state of systemd: 2026 edition is subscriber-only until 22 October 2026 and therefore only reports what can be verified: the session took place at All Systems Go! 2026 on 30 September in Berlin with maintainers Luca Boccassi and Zbigniew Jedrzejewski-Szmek giving the traditional state of the project overview, followed by a maintainer round table with Boccassi, Jedrzejewski-Szmek, Daan De Meyer and Lennart Poettering addressing systemd's size, health and whether it might replace Kubernetes (it will not), plus the verifiable fact that v262 shipped on 23 September with the ability to build systemd as a single statically linked multicall binary for small containers, support for the kernel coredump socket protocol introduced in Linux 6.17 and OpenSSL 4 support, and a community comment noting the static multicall binary is impressive because dlopen() long stood in the way; it deliberately refuses to summarise the round table positions it could not read. Closes by arguing the only one of the three with a hard deadline where inaction causes real breakage is the certificate lifetime change, that the most actionable advice in all three pieces is to grep for hardcoded renewal numbers because it takes minutes and immediately surfaces problems, and that the recurring theme is a shift of operational cost from fixing things when they break to keeping things continuously running.

- [Windows Update 换证书：Win7 早就没补丁了，Win10 却还有个到 2027 年 10 月的活口](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-10-09_windows-update-certificate-rotation-2027/): Translation+analysis of Microsoft's Windows IT Pro Blog post 'Prepare for Windows Update certificate rotation in 2027' (8 October 2026, Andrew Brown), covering the official mechanics and the per-version action table. Explains that Windows Update uses certificate-based trust to confirm devices connect to authoritative servers, that a set of certificates expires on 17 May 2027 and 19 June 2027, that most devices are served by normal monthly updates while some versions need IT action, and that the change does not apply to devices receiving updates through WSUS. Reproduces the action table in full: Windows 11 25H2 and later require nothing; Windows 11 24H2 and Windows Server 2025 need the September 2025 security update or later before 19 June 2027; other in-support Windows 11 versions, Windows Server 2022 and in-support Windows 10 versions need the July 2026 security update or later before 19 June 2027; LTSB/LTSC releases (Windows 10 Enterprise 2019 LTSC, Windows Server 2019 and 2016) must act before the earlier 17 May 2027 date; and other Windows versions should be upgraded because they will lose Windows Update access entirely. Covers the three post-expiration outcomes (supported and updated devices continue uninterrupted; supported but out-of-date devices lose Windows Update access but can install the required updates from the Microsoft Update Catalog; unsupported versions lose access and receive no updates), the recommended three-step action plan for IT admins, and Microsoft's own note that there is still time. Then separates this from the commonly confused Secure Boot certificate expiration starting June 2026, where devices still boot, run and receive regular updates but lose early-boot security protections, unlike the 2027 rotation which cuts off the update distribution channel itself. Answers the central question of whether Windows 7 and Windows 10 will receive no security updates at all, showing the two systems differ entirely: Windows 7 security updates and technical support ended on 14 January 2020 with paid ESU ending January 2023, so 2027 only closes the update channel a machine that has been unpatched for six years was using, with the practical pain falling on reinstalling or freshly patching such machines; while Windows 10 consumers were quietly given an extra year, with the free consumer ESU extended to 12 October 2027 (originally 13 October 2026) according to reporting, meaning ESU patches keep arriving and carry the new certificates, and the certificate deadline falls before ESU ends. Notes that Microsoft's documentation remains inconsistent across language versions, with some pages still stating the October 2026 end date, as corroboration of the quiet extension; and lists the escalation options with costs (free consumer ESU to October 2027, enterprise ESU up to three years at roughly USD 427 per device, third-party micropatching such as 0patch at about EUR 75 Pro or EUR 105 Enterprise for three years with vendor claims of support to October 2030, Windows 11 upgrade, Linux or ChromeOS Flex, or full isolation). Explains why the WSUS exemption cannot solve the underlying problem, since WSUS is only a distribution channel and no new patches exist for unsupported versions. Provides a four-question framework for deciding whether to move to Linux (are there equivalents for the critical software, is the machine personal or production, are there viable alternatives, and does the owner accept taking on maintenance responsibility), sets out the scale from Statcounter (Windows 10 about 27.8 percent, Windows 7 about 0.55 percent, Windows 11 about 71.5 percent as of September 2026), HP's investor-call figure of roughly 30 percent of its customers still on Windows 10, Lansweeper sampling of 17 to 22 percent with 23 percent in healthcare and 18 percent in manufacturing, and Canalys estimating about 240 million PCs unable to upgrade to Windows 11, and cautions that Linux distributions avoid this specific certificate rotation but have their own lifecycles, so switching solves hardware exclusion rather than software maintenance in general. Closes by treating the rotation as routine maintenance rather than a zero-day crisis, arguing the real concern is devices already running unpatched today.

- [Deno 团队加入 Cloudflare：runtime 一年后停更，Deploy 六个月后关停](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-10-09_deno-joins-cloudflare/): Translation+analysis of the 9 October 2026 announcements on both the Deno and Cloudflare blogs that the entire Deno team is joining Cloudflare to merge celld and workerd into a first-class, self-hostable runtime for Workers and Durable Objects. Sets out the concrete consequences stated on the Deno side: the Deno runtime will be supported for another year with monthly releases containing bug fixes and security updates, after which Deno Land will end its development of the runtime (it stays open source and others are welcome to continue it); Deno Deploy will keep operating for six months before shutting down, with migration support for paying customers moving to Cloudflare Workers; JSR continues operating with its infrastructure moving to Cloudflare; and rusty_v8 continues to be supported with work toward integrating it into workerd - translating to deadlines of roughly April 2027 for Deploy and October 2027 for the runtime. Explains the technical motivation through Ryan Dahl's own narrative: the 2009 Berlin IRC demo was single-server and single-threaded, and scaling it means spreading channels across machines while also storing message history and accounts; Durable Objects provided the missing abstraction as a distributed singleton with a SQLite database, single-threaded JavaScript execution, WebSocket handling and synchronous local SQLite access, so one DO per chat channel shards both data and connections; but workerd's Durable Objects support is single-instance only, which is why he started celld to build the distributed, self-hostable version. Describes celld (Apache-2.0, announced August 2026, V8 + SQLite + LTX + Tokio, a 58 MB static binary, one external dependency on object storage) and its published characteristics: RPO=0 with zero acknowledged writes lost on kill, about 90 ms durable write latency, about 20 s failover with zero data loss, 0.2/0.3 ms p50/p99 stateless latency, roughly 94k req/s per worker thread, 0.47 MB RAM per resident cell, 2,500 cells on an 8 GB node, about USD 0.02 per resident cell-month, and near-zero inactive cost - alongside its own citation of a July 2026 third-party report scoring Cloudflare's Durable Objects 2 out of 10 for reliability with the line 'technically impressive, operationally terrifying', and its honest caveat that self-hosting gives control but does not guarantee reliability. Covers Kenton Varda's rebuttal of the widely circulated lock-in theory (that Workers was made deliberately different to trap users): he argues Workers is different because it is better, that pricing is not a trick but a genuinely more efficient architecture whose savings are passed on, that without an escape hatch large customers like Shopify would never have signed, that workerd is open source and is the same code running in production rather than a parallel implementation, that former customers have migrated away using it and that is acceptable, and - most candidly - that workerd has always had a production-readiness gap because its Durable Objects support is single-instance only, that the production routing implementation is a beast unsuitable for self-hosters, and that he attempted to build the alternative last spring and embarrassingly did not succeed. Notes the plan for Ryan Dahl and Bert Belder to lead merging celld's code and ideas back into workerd. Documents the community reaction centred not on the technical merits but on disclosure asymmetry, quoting Simon Willison's widely endorsed point that the runtime sunset is in the Deno post but goes unmentioned in the Cloudflare post, along with user complaints about burying the detail, teams forced to begin migration, the observation that both meaningful Node alternatives have now been absorbed by large companies, and the telling fact that some readers initially assumed the move meant Deno was getting a second wind. Closes with three takeaways: open-source licences guarantee the right to continue rather than that anyone will, so open source is not evidence of sustainability; the lock-in rebuttal is credible precisely because it admits the gap between intent and capacity, and Workers' portability only became verifiable once an independent implementation existed; and for announcements of this shape, read the departing party's timeline rather than the acquiring party's strategy narrative.
  - Key topics: Deno, Deno Deploy, Deno runtime, Cloudflare, Workers, Durable Objects, celld, workerd, rusty_v8, JSR, Ryan Dahl, Kenton Varda, Bert Belder, SQLite, LTX, Litestream, V8, Tokio, self-hosting, vendor lock-in, open source sustainability, Shopify, Workers for Platforms, acquisition, Hacker News, Simon Willison, 译文

- [Snapdragon X 笔记本的 Linux HDR 支持来了：静态 HDR10，补丁是 LLM 辅助写的](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-10-09_qualcomm-msm-drm-hdr/): Translation+analysis of Phoronix's report that Qualcomm's MSM DRM kernel driver is gaining static HDR support for DisplayPort outputs and eDP panels, benefiting Snapdragon X laptops running Linux. Frames why this matters: HDR is a real gap on ARM laptops under Linux whose absence degrades video playback, gaming and colour grading to SDR without an obvious error, and it illustrates the way ARM laptop Linux support advances through individual driver features rather than one big release - alongside s2idle suspend, Freedreno/Turnip GPU work and thermal binning patches - so the practical way to judge readiness is counting what remains (camera/ISP paths, fingerprint, audio codec coverage, dock compatibility) rather than trusting vendor support roadmaps. Explains the static-versus-dynamic HDR distinction and why the limitation matters: static HDR applies one set of metadata to an entire piece of content (HDR10, HLG) while dynamic HDR varies per scene or frame (HDR10+, Dolby Vision) and requires metadata parsing plus dynamic mapping, so this patch builds the signal path and colour-space handling rather than solving how highlights map to a panel's actual brightness. - [ext4 弃用 data=journal：最「安全」的那个挂载模式，2028 年要走了](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-10-09_ext4-deprecates-data-journal/): Translation+analysis of Phoronix's report that ext4 has deprecated its journaled data=journal mount mode, merged during the Linux 7.3 merge window (commit 6c377d19d4a5116d9bec5203aa3c6c11523e7898) with removal planned for 2028, after the 2027 Linux LTS kernel. Explains what the mode does (all file data and metadata written to the journal before being committed to the main filesystem, so the journal can be replayed to recover data after a crash or power loss), why it was chosen (it suits users very concerned about data integrity and safety) and its costs as stated in the coverage: significant write performance penalties versus the default data=ordered or data=writeback, plus delayed allocation and Direct I/O support being disabled - the latter mattering for databases and virtual machine images that depend on bypassing the page cache. Adds the three-mode comparison from the kernel documentation: writeback journals no data at all and can leave incorrect data in recently written files after a crash but typically performs best; ordered (the default) journals only metadata yet logically groups data-related metadata with the data blocks in one transaction and writes the associated data blocks first, performing slightly slower than writeback but significantly faster than journal; and journal providing full data and metadata journaling. Notes the documentation's explicit framing that the default mode does not guarantee file data blocks are in any consistent state after a crash, which is precisely the question data=journal answers, and covers fast commits in data=ordered mode storing only the minimal delta needed to recreate affected metadata in space shared with JBD2, which helps explain why the default holds up. Then the supplementary operations section: why the deprecation is technically reasonable (very few users paying for special-case paths in a hot subsystem, with consistency increasingly handled above the filesystem by database WAL and fsync semantics, copy-on-write filesystems using checksums and transactions, and application-level idempotency and replay, while double-writing all data became a poor trade on NVMe where write amplification affects both endurance and performance), and what administrators should do: inventory data=journal across /etc/fstab, systemd mount units, configuration management templates and /proc/mounts; judge whether it is still necessary, since the original reason may no longer exist; evaluate real alternatives rather than blindly switching to data=ordered; and treat the roughly two-year window as a real deadline aligned with distribution upgrades or hardware refreshes. Warns against assuming deprecation requires no action, since the typical path is kernel warnings, then tightened distribution configurations, then a mount failure in 2028 - making a forgotten fstab option a potential boot-time incident, and noting that a mount option sleeping in fstab for a decade suggests the system's configuration was never genuinely reviewed.
  - Key topics: ext4, filesystem, Linux kernel, data=journal, data=ordered, data=writeback, journaling, jbd2, fast commits, delayed allocation, Direct I/O, O_DIRECT, write amplification, data integrity, crash consistency, fsync, write-ahead log, copy-on-write filesystem, Btrfs, ZFS, NVMe, SSD endurance, deprecation, Linux 7.3, Linux LTS 2027, fstab, mount options, operations, Phoronix, 译文

- [Linux swap 子系统要删掉那张「交换映射表」：省下的是 1TB 交换文件里的 256MB](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-10-09_linux-swap-table-removing-swap-map/): Translation+analysis of Jonathan Corbet's LWN article on Kairui Song's modernisation of the Linux swap subsystem, the second in a series. Explains the target: the swap map, defined as an unsigned char array with one byte per slot storing the reference count, where the complications live in bit allocation - bit six (0x40) is SWAP_HAS_CACHE marking that a slot has a page assigned, 0x3f is SWAP_MAP_BAD for bad storage, and the resulting maximum reference count is 62 (SWAP_MAP_MAX). Notes that SWAP_HAS_CACHE doubles as a bit lock, with the thread that succeeds in setting it proceeding, which produced delay-and-retry loops and years of bugs; and describes the baroque overflow design (set 0x80 COUNT_CONTINUED, zero the count, allocate a new page supplying eight more significant bits, link it via the LRU list head in the associated page structures, and repeat on further overflow) while preserving the article's point that the motivation for this design is documented nowhere. Covers the first preparatory change, removing the swap bypass added by Minchan Kim in 4.15 (with SWP_SYNCHRONOUS_IO set and a reference count of one, swap-in happens synchronously with no readahead and the page is not added to the swap cache) on the grounds that the swap table made swap-cache operations fast enough that bypassing it has no real value, that readahead control is now separated and essentially disabled for fast devices, and that all swap I/O through the swap cache simplifies code and reduces race conditions - with the notable functional side effect that large multi-page folios can previously only be swapped in intact when the reference count was one, so removing bypass lifts that restriction. Then the second change, deleting SWAP_HAS_CACHE once the swap cache owns concurrency management and the remaining purpose of marking allocated-but-zero-reference slots is eliminated on both the swap-out side (folio added to the swap cache immediately on slot assignment) and the swap-in side (zero-reference slots freed immediately on removal). Documents the end goal of phase three, eliminating the swap map entirely by moving reference counting into the swap table with a five-way entry format (zero for empty; bit zero set for a shadow entry with the count in the upper bits; bottom two bits 10 for a resident folio storing the page-frame number rather than the address to make room for the count; bottom three bits 100 for a pointer entry, unused in this series; bottom four bits 1000 for a bad slot), the resulting savings (about 30 percent of the subsystem's metadata overhead gone, 256 MB saved for a 1 TB swap file, and the unification of swap map and swap cache), the larger counts available (x86_64 needs 40 bits for the PFN plus two for the resident marker, leaving 22 bits) and the simpler overflow handling (the complex multi-level mechanism removed in favour of allocating an array of unsigned long counts for the entire cluster). Notes the progress state as of the original February 2026 writing (phase two in mm-unstable and linux-next, possibly merged for 7.0; phase three in second revision with little review feedback) and the planned continuation into cgroup swap limits, plus a caution that the article predates the current 7.3 mainline. Closes with why it matters: debt repaid in the right order (bypass removable because swap cache got faster, SWAP_HAS_CACHE removable because the intermediate state was eliminated, swap map removable because its last function found a new home), the shift in swap's assumptions now that memory compression schemes like zram and faster media mean swap I/O is no longer slow and readahead can hurt.
  - Key topics: Linux kernel, swap, memory management, swap map, swap table, swap cluster, SWAP_HAS_CACHE, COUNT_CONTINUED, SWAP_MAP_BAD, SWAP_MAP_MAX, swap bypass, SWP_SYNCHRONOUS_IO, readahead, swap cache, folio, large folios, page-frame number, shadow entry, Kairui Song, Tencent, mm-unstable, linux-next, Linux 7.0, cgroup swap limits, zram, LWN, Jonathan Corbet, 译文

- [「Linux 桌面永远成功不了」这句话，2026 年该改口了：但作者抱怨的那些事是真的](https://freelamp.com/articles/2026-10-09_linux-desktop-not-expecting-experts/): Analysis and partial rebuttal of a LinuxLinks opinion piece arguing that Linux will never succeed on the desktop until it stops expecting users to be experts. Agrees with the central argument - that the community applies an odd test where being unable to repair a broken package, parse a terminal error or name your graphics session means Linux is not for you, which comes across as a daft way to promote an operating system - and preserves its strongest material: the analogy that nobody proudly announces their washing machine only works if you can interpret diagnostic codes and edit a configuration file; the separation of capability from needless complication (a capable terminal is a strength and nobody sensible proposes removing it, but trouble starts when command-line workarounds substitute for fixing rough edges in the graphical experience); the refusal to make Linux a pale imitation of Windows; and the formulation that a computer should reward curiosity without demanding it, so you should not have to muck about with the plumbing just to print a document. Highlights the author's own example as the strongest evidence, since he has used Linux for years yet spent far too long on blurry screenshots caused by fractional scaling on a 4K monitor, which reframes the issue from a user-competence problem to a product defect. Then disagrees with the headline using 2026 data: Statcounter puts Linux at 8.88 percent of the global desktop market (September), up from 7.53 percent in July and 5.59 percent in June, with 10.65 percent in North America, 18.19 percent in the United States (up from just over 10 percent in early August) and 7.78 percent in Japan, while Valve's Steam survey shows Linux at 3.90 percent overall and, within Linux, SteamOS Holo at 22.83 percent, CachyOS at 14.03 percent and Bazzite at 7.28 percent, with CachyOS topping DistroWatch's twelve-month hit ranking. Notes the measurement caveats (bots accounted for 23.44 percent of traffic in Statcounter's sample and are removed from the main statistics, and Valve's survey is opt-in) and the irony that the growth is driven by Valve and Steam Deck, an environment where users need not know their graphics session or repair packages. Identifies the gap the article does not address: who pays for 'not requiring experts', since OpenTWEAK-style edge cases such as 4K fractional scaling are fixed by sustained paid engineering, which is why Steam Deck, RHEL and Ubuntu LTS desktops fare better while consumer community distributions lack a funding model for unglamorous work. Closes with the argument that the problem is not community attitude but incentives, and that Valve has demonstrated the viable path.
